articles.title: US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages
articles.summary: As Democrats flag AI bank breaches and cyber-attacks in Japan, Jay Clayton says system failures happen

blocks.text: A bipartisan pair of US senators are calling on Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to identify and fix vulnerabilities in the US’s infrastructure following nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies.

Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce, science, and transportation committee, and Mike Rounds, the Republican chair of the Senate subcommittee on cybersecurity, sent a letter to Clayton on Tuesday, outlining concerns sparked by reports of AI accessing major banks, cyber-attacks in Japan and more.

“The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond,” Cantwell and Rounds wrote to Clayton, who is also serving as the White House AI czar.
“Even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services,” the senators wrote.

Over the last week, tech outages at major banks, workplace communication systems and even federal infrastructure like the Federal Aviation Administration – triggering a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage that grounded or delayed thousands of flights – have raised alarms about potential cyber-attacks.
Top officials have insisted the disruptions stem from software patch updates that intend to address potential AI harms.

“Many people are patching their systems. They know that they’re legacy systems, have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated,” Clayton told CNBC on Tuesday. “It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure and as you patch and upgrade your systems, taking them down and bringing them back up, there are things like this that happen.”

Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate intelligence committee, echoed Clayton. “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” he wrote on X.
Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, attempted to quell public speculation and fear by assuring Americans that the tech outages were not linked to one another or the work of malicious actors.

But nationwide cyber outages have roiled the country, filled with voters who are already skeptical of rapidly integrating and developing AI. It is unclear what exactly has caused the widespread outages or if AI played a role.
JD Vance canceled his scheduled interview at the New York Times’ DealBook summit on Wednesday, citing his need to attend meetings addressing the recent tech outages.

Cantwell and Rounds are asking Clayton to provide cybersecurity tools to critical US infrastructure such as hospitals, utilities, small government, federal agencies and more, to prevent further disruptions.

They are also asking that US cybersecurity teams secure the same AI systems that are deployed to find vulnerabilities in software, raising concerns that they can “gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems”.

articles.title: Bacterial toxin produced by E coli leading suspect in rise in bowel cancer among under-50s
articles.summary:
Scientists tell Commons committee that exposure to colibactin in early life is a potential driver of early onset colorectal cancer

Exposure to a bacterial toxin in early life has emerged as…

blocks.text: Exposure to a bacterial toxin in early life has emerged as a leading suspect in the rise of bowel cancer amongs those under 50, MPs have heard.

Cases of early onset bowel cancer have doubled in many countries in the past two decades, and while rising obesity and a fall in physical activity are contributors, researchers believe other factors must also be involved.

Dr Karl Smith-Byrne, a senior molecular epidemiologist at the University of Oxford, told the Commons science and technology committee that known risk factors for colorectal cancer, such as obesity, smoking and alcohol, can explain only about half of the cases doctors diagnose.
He said he did not find it “plausible” that the rise in early onset bowel cancer could be entirely explained by risk factors that researchers were already aware of.

Last year scientists identified a toxin called colibactin, produced by some variants of E coli bacteria in the gut, as a potential driver of early onset colorectal cancer. Hallmark mutations caused by the toxin were three times more common in tumours from people under 40 than in those from people over 70.

More work is needed to understand whether colibactin actually drives bowel cancer, but it is a question scientists are now actively pursuing. “That’s probably the leading explanation at the moment,” Smith-Byrne told MPs.

Prof Mike Stratton at the Sanger Institute, who was not at the hearing, has said that colibactin causes mutations in some children but not others, with evidence of mutations appearing as early as infancy. By the age of 10, affected children can have a similar “mutational burden” to a 50-year-old, his work showed.

“If it is causing mutations, it’s causing mutations at a sensitive period earlier in life, and that can give that person’s colon or their rectum a head start on its journey towards being cancerous or developing these tumours,” said Smith-Byrne, who is himself a survivor of early onset rectal cancer.

Some suspect that particular variants of E coli that normally live harmlessly in the gut have evolved in recent decades to produce colibactin. Prof Elio Riboli, a cancer epidemiologist at Imperial College London, told the committee: “This colibactin is essentially found in people born after 1960. Something has happened in the E coli bacteria … There must have been a mutation, and there is a new bacteria.”

Bowel cancer is the third most common cancer in the world, accounting for about one in 10 of all cases. The disease is still far more common in the over-50s, but global figures suggest diagnoses are rising steeply in younger people.

Prof Helen Coleman, a cancer epidemiologist at Queen’s University Belfast, told MPs that colibactin was “the first new clue that we’ve had in quite some time”, but that its potential role in bowel cancer was still under investigation.

“Even though we’re talking about adults that are being diagnosed with cancer between 18 and 49, it’s quite likely to be very early life exposures,” she said. “It could be something you were exposed to in very early childhood, possibly even in the prenatal period, and that makes it very difficult to study.”

Riboli said that while scientists need to uncover the unknown drivers of different cancers, people should minimise risks that are already clear. In the UK and US, drinking and smoking are both falling, but obesity is rising and physical activity is in decline. “The quick win could come from applying what we know,” he said. “We could prevent about 60% of the cancers occurring now, but we are not applying in society what we know.”

articles.title: Anti-vaccine group once led by RFK Jr back on Facebook and Instagram after being banned
articles.summary:
Children’s Health Defense was removed from Facebook and Instagram in 2022. Meta declined to comment on why it allowed the group back

An anti-vaccine group led for years by Robert F Kennedy…

blocks.text: An anti-vaccine group led for years by Robert F Kennedy Jr has been allowed back on Facebook and Instagram, four years after Meta removed the group for repeatedly violating its misinformation policies.

A review by the Guardian found that Children’s Health Defense (CHD) has reopened or opened six accounts on Facebook and Instagram from May through September this year. The group is using its accounts to share false and misleading information about topics including vaccines and deadly measles outbreaks at a time when measles has come roaring back. Health officials have reported 10 measles-associated deaths in the United States this year, and the country this week lost its measles elimination status in an official recognition that it is again endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.

The CHD news comes after a Guardian investigation this month found health and vaccine misinformation was rampant on Facebook in a massive public group, Crunchy Moms, and that Facebook was recommending it to users despite apparent violations of its policies. Crunchy Moms was started a few months after Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg last year announced a rollback of moderation and factchecking. Zuckerberg defended the move at the time by saying he wanted to restore “free expression on our platforms”.
Kennedy now serves as the US health secretary, and CHD continues to have close ties to him. He headlined their annual conference in September.

The group was removed from both Facebook and Instagram by Meta in 2022, after years of criticism that Kennedy and his group were top spreaders of false information about vaccines, Covid-19 and other topics on the platforms. Meta said at the time it “removed these accounts for repeatedly violating our policies”, and told CHD it was because its accounts went against community standards on “misinformation that could cause physical harm”.

In 2023, Meta restored Kennedy’s Instagram account, which he had lost in 2021 for sharing false information about Covid and vaccines. The company said it made the decision because Kennedy was an active candidate for US president. But it also said it would not restore CHD’s accounts.
Meta declined to comment on why it allowed CHD back on its platforms and why it was allowing apparent violations of its misinformation policy by CHD.
CHD did not respond to requests for comment.

Kennedy frequently tussled with Facebook before he entered the government. CHD sued Facebook in 2020, when Kennedy was leading the group, claiming it was being censored. The case was dismissed the following year, with the judge finding that Facebook, as a private entity, could not be held liable for violating the group’s constitutional rights. Earlier this year, the Washington Sun reported that Meta’s lawyer argued in a lawsuit in New Mexico that the judge should consider Kennedy’s trustworthiness and “unusual” views on vaccines when urging it not to enter a government-produced report into evidence in a lawsuit over the company’s child safety practices.

Dorit Reiss, a professor at UC Law San Francisco who has closely monitored CHD’s legal cases, said she did not believe there was a legal reason that Meta would be compelled to put CHD back on its platforms, and that it was possible Meta had simply made a political calculation and ceased to enforce its own anti-misinformation policies.
“Facebook has the right to decide what to do here,” Reiss said. “Meta decided it’s more profitable … that it’s more in their interest to let the misinformers back up.”
The Guardian found several posts on the reinstated and new CHD accounts that appear to violate Meta’s harmful health misinformation policy.

A video posted recently by one of its Facebook accounts is titled: “Vaccines: Your child could die,” and makes the misleading claim that vaccines are deadly. Another one earlier this month said: “Somehow there’s this narrative, vaccines are safe and effective, and we know that’s just a lie.”

A video posted last month to at least two of its accounts says of the six measles-associated deaths reported in Pennsylvania at that time: “None of them died from the measles.” Another said the MMR vaccine is “not so safe and effective”. Another said none of the vaccines ever eliminated any epidemic in history.

Another post this month suggested it was unsafe to follow doctors’ recommendations to get multiple vaccinations at once. A June 2026 video posted by the account says the HPV vaccines are “very dangerous”, have “caused hundreds, thousands of deaths” and do not prevent cervical cancer.

articles.title: What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
articles.summary: When "GTA VI" is released on November 19, millions of people worldwide will rush to their consoles to play it. How has this video game created such a cross-generational buzz?

image.caption: Lucia and Jason are the protagonists of 'Grand Theft Auto VI': For the first time in the franchise's main titles, gamers can play as a womanImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: "Oh, it's so on now!" is the tagline in the latest trailer for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI" for short.

"GTA VI" is a game of superlatives that's been crashing through records. The hype around it is unparalleled. No game in history has clocked so many pre-orders. It's thought that around 10 million people have already purchased it. There's no denying it: "GTA VI" is a global cultural phenomenon.

A few days before its release on November 19, fans can already start downloading the game. The file is so large that downloading it can take several days, depending on the internet connection. Providers have already registered a significant spike in data traffic.
As soon as the game is unlocked, players can start speeding through the fictional US metropolis of Vice City in a stylish sports car with criminal couple Jason and Lucia.
Miami gets cast as Vice City

To mark the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," its real-life inspiration — Miami — is getting a full-scale "Vice City" makeover. This promotional push includes the Miami Heat basketball team stepping onto the hardwood in custom "Vice City" jerseys for a home game, a local festival featuring artists from the game's official soundtrack, and roadside "Vice City" signage installed across the area.

blocks.caption: Vice City is a fictionalized representation of the US metropolis of MiamiImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Expectations for "GTA VI" are sky-high. Nearly 5,000 people have been working on the game for more than 10 years. Development costs are estimated at around $1 billion (€900 million).

"Based on those figures alone — as well as the series' extremely successful and popular track record — this can certainly be described as a truly exceptional release," says Rudolf Thomas Inderst, cultural studies scholar and professor of Game Design and Game Studies at Germany's Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences.

When such an effort is put into a product, it's only natural for people to expect great things, he adds. Inderst is expecting "GTA VI" to showcase the absolute best of what modern gaming can do across gameplay, storytelling, visuals and tech.
Social satire and gameplay freedom

This video game series has been around for almost three decades, setting new standards through its different versions. A biting satire on US society and the American dream, "GTA" parodies politics, culture and the media.

The game is also renowned for its gameplay freedom and spectacularly staged chaos in a crazy world where players can do whatever they please. Shoot down helicopters with a bazooka, go to the hairdresser's, take a stroll on the beach, go to a nightclub, take part in car races and much more.

blocks.caption: Pure escapism: In Vice City, there's shooting and dancingImage: Rockstar Games/dpa Picture Alliance

blocks.text: What makes it a standout among video games is how its NPCs — non-player characters, those not being controlled by a human player — are brought to life. They respond based on a player's interactions with them, displaying individualized behaviors and traits ranging from fear to hostility. "GTA VI" has an estimated 600,000 animations for the civilians in the fictional state of Leonida.
'Grand Theft Auto,' a long-running hit

"GTA VI" is essentially a huge adult playground, striking a chord across several generations. Millennials grew up with "Grand Theft Auto III," "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City," "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas," and "Grand Theft Auto IV," while Gen Z grew up with "Grand Theft Auto V." Generation Alpha might still be too young for the latest edition, but will likely find ways to play it anyway.

blocks.caption: In 'GTA VI,' Lucia and Jason play a gangster couple; the players' actions determine how close they becomeImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Social media has certainly played a part in the series' ongoing success, particularly "GTA V" and its multiplayer spin-off, "GTA Online." Numerous content creators stream gameplay sessions on Twitch or YouTube, and particularly funny or crazy gameplay moments end up on TikTok.

At the same time, a dedicated role-play community has grown around the game. Players gather inside the world of "GTA" to act out specific characters, such as taxi drivers, judges or small-time criminals. They invent realistic backstories for their personas, and many even use accents to stay in character.
Perfectionism has its downsides

The hype surrounding "GTA VI" is not only good news for the game itself but could also boost the entire games industry by drawing more people back to their consoles. This is because the boom triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic was followed by studio closures and redundancies. Worldwide, it's estimated that 50,000 people in the games industry have lost their jobs since 2022.

But while publisher Rockstar Games is well-known for the meticulous polish of its titles and attention to detail, the perfectionism so prized by fans also has its drawbacks, especially for those working on the game. Rockstar, like many other game developers, has frequently faced major criticism regarding its labor practices.

blocks.caption: 'GTA' characters can relax at Leonida Keys, but game developers face high-pressure workloads in the lead-up to game releasesImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Former developers report extremely long working hours and a heavy workload that resulted in health issues. Trade unions accuse company managers of employee surveillance, resulting in a culture of workplace stress and low morale.

Coinciding with the launch of Rockstar's largest game to date, the developers behind it are pushing for trade union recognition. That move would give them a collective voice to address working hours, pay, pensions and parental leave. If successful, their campaign could set a major precedent for the wider video game industry, which continues to face challenges around fair labor practices.
This article was originally written in German.
Hooked on video gaming

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries poised to become 1st Black U.S. House Speaker, after internal vote by Democrats
articles.summary: Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the country's first Black American…

image.caption: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks with reporters at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. (Jose Luis Magana/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the country's first Black American with the gavel.
Full vote in House, including Republican members, will take place in early January

Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the country's first Black American with the gavel.

Jeffries, of New York, secured the nod during closed-door voting, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress, including Republican members, convenes in January. CNN reported that there were 11 No votes out of 262 cast.
The speaker of the House is second in the presidential line of succession, behind the vice-president.
Jeffries ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in the recent midterm elections in a rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump and the party in power.

Phone calls and social media posts have been flooding the offices of returning Democrats and newly elected members demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver.

Ahead of Wednesday's vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. He met with the caucuses that make up the House Democrats and talked to almost all members in what will be their large majority.
"I embrace those conversations," he said.
Elevated to leader in 12 years

Jeffries will be part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, which would also represent historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed.

items: Investigate Trump or work with him? Democrats debate best path forward
Mary Peltola wins U.S. Senate seat in Alaska for Democrats

blocks.text: Jeffries, 56, was born in Brooklyn to a mother who was a social worker and a father who was a substance abuse counsellor. He attended Binghamton University for undergraduate studies, earning a master's in public policy from Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., and a law degree from New York University.
After two unsuccessful bids for a state assembly seat in New York, he succeeded in 2006. He was elected to U.S. Congress eight years later, joining the Congressional Caucus.
Chuck Schumer facing challenge for U.S. Senate leadership

There are seven races yet to be projected in the 435-seat House of Representatives. Democrats have sewn up 257 seats, and with one of the biggest incoming majorities in decades, Jeffries will have room to spare, unlike current Speaker Mike Johnson from the Republicans.

When Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California decided to step aside from leadership in 2022 after the party's electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this era. Pelosi, No. 2 Democratic Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland and Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina had often moved together, rising, and then stepping back, from their long-held positions.
Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders of the post-Pelosi era and will soon serve as leaders in the majority for the first time.

"There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries," Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said at the Capitol. "I think that everyone is far more concerned what that leadership means, what is it promising."

items: Maryland's Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for U.S. Senate leadership post
How the Democrats' midterm wave shows a path back to the presidency

blocks.text: The Senate Democrats will decide on their leader early next month. Chuck Schumer of New York, who has been majority leader before, faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland.
Returning Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona said the situations in the Senate and the House "are quite different."
She said Jeffries has been a collaborative leader who is listening to ideas from progressive caucus members like her and others.
"His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction," Ansari said.
"It is more productive to focus on preparing on what we're going to do in the majority and what we need and want to get done in those first 100 days."
With files from CBC News

articles.title: California Republicans won only four of state’s 52 US House seats in midterms
articles.summary:
California Democrats flipped five seats and will send 48 representatives to DC after successful redistricting effort

California Republicans have taken an extraordinary hit in the midterm…

blocks.text: California Republicans have taken an extraordinary hit in the midterm elections, with only four of the state’s 52 congressional seats going to GOP representatives, leaving the party with its smallest delegation to Washington in decades.

California Democrats flipped five seats and will be sending 48 representatives to Washington DC for the new term. The result stems from the successful redistricting effort spearheaded by the state’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, as well as a seismic blue wave has knocked out Republicans across the country in districts that previously backed Donald Trump.
The last time California Republicans held only four House seats was in 1937 when the state had just 20 total congressional representatives, according to CalMatters, a local news site.
Democrats have long been in the majority in California, the most populous state in the US, but conservative regions in the state have remained strongholds for Republican candidates.

Republicans held on to one seat in the state’s central valley, one in northern California near the Oregon border, one east of Los Angeles and one that that includes parts of Orange county in the southern region.
Before the midterms, Republicans held eight congressional seats in California.

In the state’s central valley, progressive Democrat Randy Villegas, a community college professor, ousted a six-term Republican, David Valadao, in a redrawn district. Villegas had shunned corporate campaign donations and was endorsed by national progressive leaders, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders.

In southern California, Democrat Marni von Wilpert beat Republican Jim Desmond, who had been endorsed by Trump, flipping a seat that was redrawn to favor Democrats. Von Wilpert, whose campaign focused on workers’ rights and affordability, will represent the state’s 48th district, previously held by Darrell Issa, a longtime Republican congressman who chose not to run for re-election after the maps were redrawn.

The final race called by the Associated Press in the state was for a Republican incumbent, Jay Obernolte, who narrowly defeated his Democratic opponent, Tessa Lynn Hodge, in a region east of LA. Obernolte won with only 50.8% of the vote despite running in a Republican-majority district.

The Democrats’ successes in the Golden State came after voters overwhelmingly supported Proposition 50, a redistricting measure meant to counter Republicans’ partisan gerrymandering in Texas. Across the country, Republicans’ efforts to redraw districts in their favor spectacularly backfired, with the party failing to pick up nearly all the seats they redrew.

articles.title: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
articles.summary: Watch: The BBC's Jonathan Beale joins Ukrainian forces who have taken the battle below ground and out of sight of Russian drones.

blocks.text: For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.

With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.
Read Jonathan Beale's dispatch from the front line.

articles.title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
articles.summary: Ukrainian forces are fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet tunnel in the Kharkiv region.

blocks.text: Watch: Inside the gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
ByJonathan Beale
Defence correspondent, near Kupyansk
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

blocks.caption: Map showing the location of a gas pipeline in north-eastern Ukraine near Kupyansk. A red line marks the pipeline running from east to west to the north of the Kupyansk. The map indicates that the area in the north east of the map is currently under Russian military control. This area is extended…

blocks.text: Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.

The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Troops move through the tunnel on special sleds - they call it the Kupyansk metro

blocks.text: Image source, Moose Campbell/BBC
Troops move through the tunnel on special sleds - they call it the Kupyansk metro
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.

They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.

Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.

Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ukrainian troops like Musician rarely see the sun - but they say they feel safer underground

blocks.text: Ukrainian troops like Musician rarely see the sun - but they say they feel safer underground
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.

But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.

Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."

His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The men live and fight in very tight quarters - but have managed to clear 15km of the pipe

blocks.text: The men live and fight in very tight quarters - but have managed to clear 15km of the pipe
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.

Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."
The battle of the pipeline is not over.

Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.

blocks.caption: A Ukrainian soldier call sign Zanuda stands in a black hoodie and black cap in front of a sign reading Khartiya

blocks.text: Moose Campbell/BBC
Ground operations are now nearly impossible... everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground

blocks.caption: "Ground operations are now nearly impossible... everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground", Source: Zanuda, Source description: Ukrainian soldier, Image: A Ukrainian soldier call sign Zanuda stands in a black hoodie and black cap in front of a sign reading Khartiya

blocks.text: While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.

But, Zanuda believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."
In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.
It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success. It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale. But on its own it has not changed the course of the war.
For Ukraine, there is still no light at the end of the tunnel.
Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Marcos in China for 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. went to China on Thursday to attend the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting a day after wrapping up Manila's chairmanship and hosting of the ASEAN Summit.

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 12:59am

APEC leaders and their spouses gather with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Madame Peng Liyuan for the official group photo at the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China. President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. and First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos join their fellow leaders and spouses for the occasion. (Photo from Presidential Communications Office)
Xi Jinping gives Marcos, FL Liza official welcome

SHENZHEN — President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos were given an official welcome by Chinese President Xi Jinping and First Lady Peng Liyuan on Wednesday evening in this city for the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting.
Marcos and First Lady Liza joined their fellow leaders and spouses tonight for a gala dinner and cultural presentation.
The event was meant for “cultural celebration, friendship, and camaraderie,” bringing together leaders and their spouses at the APEC summit,” according to the Presidential Communications Office.
Marcos and his entire delegation arrived in China at 5:30 p.m. today.
The APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held from November 18 to 19, preceded by an annual summit of CEOs on November 17 to 18.

On Thursday, Marcos is expected to have bilateral meetings with three world leaders: Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, and Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape.
Marcos' visit in China comes after the Philippines' hosting of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits from November 15 to 17, 2026.
APEC is a regional forum of 21 member economies in the Asia-Pacific. The theme of this year's summit is "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together."
More stories: https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/ Follow us: https://www.facebook.com/gmanews/
Marcos arrives in China to attend APEC Leaders' Meeting
SHENZHEN, China — President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of his participation in the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting.
The PR001 carrying the President and his delegation landed at the Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport at 5:30 p.m.
Marcos is expected to attend a gala dinner in Shenzhen tonight (Wednesday evening).

According to Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, Cabinet Secretary Benhur Abalos, and Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado Estrella III will serve as the country’s caretakers while Marcos is in China from November 18 to 20.
Xi, Putin blast Western 'protectionism,' sanctions before meeting Trump at APEC

SHENZHEN, China — China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, while his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin criticized Western sanctions as the two set the stage for a high-stakes trilateral meeting with Donald Trump.

They delivered their speeches at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, ahead of US President Trump's arrival from Manila, where he was meeting key regional allies.

The three men are due to meet on the sidelines on Thursday and potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.

The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
China's Xi calls for free and open trade at APEC CEO Summit

SHENZHEN, China - Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday urged support for "free and open trade," while expressing opposition to "protectionism" in an opening speech at an Asia-Pacific summit where he was due to meet his US and Russian counterparts.

Xi's remarks came after Washington announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, which could further complicate a fragile trade truce with Beijing. China has pledged to retaliate.

"We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains," Xi told an audience of business executives, after posing a series of rhetorical questions on how the Asia Pacific should respond to a changing world.
Western trade partners have criticized China for running annual trade surpluses in excess of $1 trillion through policies that support its manufacturing sector at the expense of its consumers.
Marcos flies to China for APEC Summit
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Wednesday afternoon left Manila to participate in the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China.
The PR001 carrying the President and his delegation left Villamor Air Base at 3:25 p.m.

With Marcos are First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, Finance Secretary Frederick Go, Trade and Industry Secretary Cristina Roque, Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, and Presidential Communications Office Secretary Lino Cayetano.
They are expected to land at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport past 5 p.m.

articles.title: Brooklyn man sues, saying he warned of cracks before deadly building collapse
articles.summary:
Dengane Omari Jack filed a lawsuit against his landlord and multiple construction companies

A Brooklyn man who lost his home in the…

blocks.text: A Brooklyn man who lost his home in the building collapse that killed eight people last week has said he raised concerns about visible cracks in the brickwork weeks before the disaster.

Dengane Omari Jack, 48, made the allegations in a lawsuit filed against his landlord and multiple construction companies after the apartment building on Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a neighboring construction site on 11 November.
Investigators are still working to establish the cause of the collapse, which claimed the lives of two children, and left several others injured.

According to the court filing, Jack had spotted cracks near the entrance of the building in October and photographed the damage before sending the pictures to his landlord. But rather than being assured that the problem would be addressed, Jack claims his concerns were dismissed.
“Plaintiff was falsely told, in substance, that the condition was not the landlord’s fault or could not be fixed,” the lawsuit said.
The collapsed apartment building stood beside an active construction site where another structure had already been demolished and excavation work was underway for a new residential development.

The lawsuit seeks to hold the landlord and construction companies connected to both properties accountable for allegedly neglecting to act on the structural concerns Jack reported before the deadly collapse.

The defendants “failed to arrange a timely and adequate structural investigation, obtain necessary protection or repairs, or take appropriate steps in response to the reported condition and the ongoing adjoining excavation”, the lawsuit said.
The former tenant is suing for reimbursement for rent he previously paid, a replacement apartment and additional financial compensation.

Jack, who works as a musician and DJ, told the New York Post he had occupied a top-floor apartment in the building for five years. He escaped the disaster because he was working at a school at the time the structure came crashing down.

An extensive music collection, which Jack had spent decades assembling, was lost in the disaster. Speaking to Gothamist, he said thousands of albums collected over about 30 years now lay beneath the rubble, with some dating back to when he emigrated to the US from St Vincent and the Grenadines as a teenager. Jack estimated the collection’s value at more than $100,000.

Built in 1930, the Brooklyn building was 96-years-old when it crumbled. Records from New York City’s department of housing, preservation, and development show the property had accumulated 98 violations dating back to 1972.

Eleven of those violations were issued within the past year, including one involving “unsafe electrical wiring” and another directing the property owner to “provide an adequate supply of water for the wet sprinkler and/or standpipe.”

The city’s Department of Buildings and law enforcement authorities have launched an investigation into the incident, focused on both the condition of the destroyed apartment building and the construction activity taking place next door.

articles.title: Nathan Fielder lookalike contest crowns a deadpan winner
articles.summary: Dozens competed in a Nathan Fielder lookalike contest in Toronto on Tuesday, taking on business pitches, a staring contest and an improvised conversation with an Elizabeth Holmes impersonator.

image.caption: Comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder, left, inspired a lookalike contest at Toronto’s Paradise Theatre on Tuesday, which was won by Jayden Daniels, right, who never broke character once onstage. (Chris Delmas/AFP via Getty Images, Mehrdad Nazarahari/CBC)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Dozens competed in a Nathan Fielder lookalike contest in Toronto on Tuesday, taking on business pitches, a staring contest and an improvised conversation with an Elizabeth Holmes impersonator.
30 contestants competed for the title at Toronto’s Paradise Theatre

Dozens of Nathan Fielder lookalikes delighted a packed audience of comedy fans at a Toronto Theatre on Tuesday night to answer a simple, if oddly specific question: Who looks most like Nathan Fielder?

Thirty contestants sporting grey wigs took part in the competition devoted to the Canadian comedian and filmmaker with the unnervingly earnest persona — known for the docu-comedies Nathan for You, The Rehearsal and the recent hit documentary You Can See Everything.
The lookalikes came dressed for the role, with some wearing headphones and button-down shirts, while others leaned into Fielder’s signature blank stare and dry delivery.

But resemblance was only part of the assignment. Over the course of the evening at the Paradise Theatre, they faced a business pitch challenge, a staring contest and a final conversation with an Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced tech executive at the centre of You Can See Everything, impersonated by Second City alumnus Hannah Spear.

The pitch round produced schemes worthy of Nathan For You, in which Fielder plays an awkward business consultant fielding extreme, absurd marketing ideas to help real struggling businesses. One lookalike contestant named David, a drummer, proposed growing his indie band's audience on Instagram without paying for ads. He said the band had 250 followers, "and statistically 40 of those are my mom’s friends" before presenting a QR code to follow the band.
Another pitch was for a celebrity lookalike contest in which winners would pay rather than collect prize money. "This is not a prize list. This is a price list," said one contestant.

Host Andrew Phung, known for Kim’s Convenience and Run the Burbs, welcomed the crowd with a suitably grand introduction, calling Fielder "a cultural icon, a Canadian pop culture phenomenon and a graduate of one of Canada’s top business schools with very good grades" — a playful nod to the opening tagline of Nathan for You and to the fact that Fielder really did earn a business degree from the University of Victoria in 2005.
Phung and Spear judged the contest alongside Kelly White and Megan Bianco, hosts of the Nathan for Us fan podcast.
Thirty contestants and fans of awkward comedy filled the Paraside Theatre on Tuesday. (Christine Pagulayan/CBC)

The judges narrowed the group to three finalists, evaluating each contestant’s appearance, costume, physicality, business pitch and improv skills. Toronto’s Jayden Williams took the crown, after staying in character throughout the competition.
"There were some Nathan ringers out there," Daniels told CBC News. "I’m shocked and flattered that I won."
Daniels said friends had repeatedly sent him a photo of the event flyer until he finally decided to enter. He also had experience: he’d already won two Halloween contests dressed as Fielder.

When asked about staying in character throughout the competition, Daniels responded with a pause and a deflection worthy of the comedian he was impersonating: "I really, I don’t know what you’re talking about."
Daniels, centre, said he’d already won two Halloween contests dressed as Fielder. (Lucky Osunbiyi Photography)

The contest attracted both longtime fans and people who had only recently discovered the comedian. Some were hooked by Fielder’s deadpan delivery; others found his comedy compelling precisely because it feels a little unsettling.
"He scares me, and that’s why I like him," one attendee said. Fielder, the fan added, seems "like an alien on Earth that’s pretending to be human."
Another fan called him "Canadian excellence," adding that his older work had found a wider audience as his profile grew.
After the winner was crowned, the crowd settled in to watch the first episode of The Curse, Fielder’s series with Benny Safdie.

items: Loved You Can See Everything? Thank Canada
Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything gazes into the abyss of Elizabeth Holmes

blocks.text: The contest arrived amid renewed attention around Fielder’s work, including You Can See Everything, the hit documentary co-directed with Lance Oppenheim that examines disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Fans at the theatre said the film had introduced them to Fielder or deepened their interest in his work.

Fielder lookalike contests have also been held in cities including New York, Los Angeles and Sydney. But for one night, Toronto’s many Nathans shared a stage, and one went home with the title, "the Nathanest Nathan," as dubbed by those on social media.
Daniels said he hoped to see more lookalike contests across more Canadian cities, including Montreal and Hamilton. "But it was nice to have one in Toronto, with one of Canada’s heroes," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Julio Iglesias facing court investigation over alleged sexual offences
articles.summary: The 83-year-old singer is accused of abusing two former employees at Caribbean residences in 2021.

blocks.text: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members
Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.
The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.
Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.

But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.
He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after the he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".
Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.
The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.
In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.
The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.
In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.
Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.
In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".
WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.

But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".

The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.
Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.
He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

articles.title: Fiona the hippo undergoing care after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
articles.summary: Zookeepers say she cannot have surgery but are providing fluids and supportive care to help her pass the hat.

blocks.text: The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure.
The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through".
But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover.
The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated.
"Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos and our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," one of the zookeepers said in an update.
Fiona was born six weeks early to 17-year-old hippo Bibi on 24 January.
At birth she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
The zoo said staff were "rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".

articles.title: AI-enabled weather forecast launched
articles.summary: Through the country’s upgraded weather forecasting with artificial intelligence, the Department of Science and Technology is aiming for stronger disaster preparedness.

blocks.text: November 19, 2026 | 12:00am

Launched Tuesday, the PANaHON app of the state weather bureau has integrated AI with the help of US-based Atmo, giving Filipinos access to more detailed, location-specific weather forecasts up to 14 days ahead.
Businessworld / ATMO.AI
MANILA, Philippines — Through the country’s upgraded weather forecasting with artificial intelligence, the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) is aiming for stronger disaster preparedness.

“This artificial intelligence-based product, which provides detailed weather information, including not just rainfall but also temperature, is extremely important during the El Niño phenomenon, especially for Filipinos who work outdoors,” DOST Secretary Renato Solidum said.
Local government units (LGUs) can provide timely guidance to constituents, especially in the agriculture, aviation and shipping sectors, Solidum stressed.

Atmo chief executive officer and co-founder Alexander Levy said the new forecasting system improves three major aspects of weather prediction: geographical detail, time precision and forecasting duration.

Up to 100 times greater geographical detail is provided by the system, allowing users to distinguish weather conditions across smaller areas, including hills, valleys and mountainous locations, Levy pointed out.
The system offers 12 times greater time precision, generating forecasts at 15-minute intervals instead of the standard three-hour intervals, he noted.

“Compared to standard forecasts that often have a time step of three hours, the new system has a time step of 15 minutes. Every hour that’s four subdivisions. This is a very high level of frequency, especially over the long duration of the forecast,” he said.
Seven weather parameters are displayed in the system: rainfall, accumulated rainfall, wind intensity, atmospheric pressure, temperature, heat index and relative humidity.
Users can select specific locations on the map to view localized forecasts and examine weather conditions through the platform’s available time intervals.
The AI model was trained and fine-tuned using historical weather data from the Philippines to account for the country’s distinct meteorological conditions, Levy said.
Climate action

Meanwhile, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) has partnered with two global climate networks to strengthen the capacity of LGUs in implementing effective climate adaptation and mitigation measures.

The DENR collaborated with the C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group and Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy to establish the Philippines Leadership on Climate Action and Localization program.

Under the PhilLOCAL program, the three bodies will work together to align local climate policies with national commitments, improve access to climate data and capacity and help LGUs develop investment-ready climate projects that can garner investments.
