articles.title: Xi, Putin meet in China, ahead of summit with Trump
articles.summary: China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, while his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin criticized Western sanctions as the two set the stage for a…

image.caption: In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping shake hands Wednesday prior to a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. (Sergei Bobylyov/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, while his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin criticized Western sanctions as the two set the stage for a high-stakes trilateral meeting with ‌U.S. President Donald Trump.
Other countries watch with great interest as leaders of 3 powers prepare to meet

They delivered their speeches at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, hours before Trump landed in China after meeting key regional allies in Manila this week.

Xi greeted Trump at the airport, reciprocating the U.S. president's gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September when they last met. They had a brief hug and a short exchange before walking along the red carpet to their motorcades.
The two will participate in an APEC group photo and attend a banquet with other leaders.

They will meet ​with Putin on the sidelines on Thursday and potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the U.S. war ​with Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.

The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-Second World War order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
What to know about Canada and China's new trade pact
It has also ​unnerved some European and Asian capitals, who fear the world's greatest military powers will disregard their interests.
The Wall Street Journal, in an editorial, said it was "a sign of Mr. Trump’s mercurial foreign policy that the [summit] is creating more anxiety among allies than adversaries."

The Kremlin this week dismissed comparisons with the Yalta Conference as "games of political scientists," but said the meeting will have a major impact on global affairs. Beijing said the trilateral will promote world peace.

items: Carney to meet with Trump at APEC, says Canada's trade ties with China are not U.S. president's top concern
Canada and China announce new trade measures and cultural partnerships on Carney's 1st day in Shenzhen

blocks.text: In his opening address, Xi urged support for what he ⁠called "free and open trade," trying to portray his ⁠country as a stable partner on the global stage, in contrast with the U.S., which has raised tariffs and ‌adopted a more muscular foreign policy under Trump.

Xi's remarks came after Washington announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, which could further complicate a fragile trade truce with Beijing. China has pledged to retaliate.

"We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains," Xi told an audience of business executives.
Dancers wave Russian and Chinese flags during the welcoming ceremony for Putin on Wednesday. (Anupam Nath/The Associated Press)
Western trade partners have ⁠criticized China for running annual trade surpluses exceeding $1 trillion US through policies that support its manufacturing sector at the expense of its consumers.

Beijing says its growth model is appropriate for an economy still catching up with the world's richest, but the U.S., the European Union in Brussels and others are concerned about China's supply chain dominance providing the country with geopolitical leverage and say its policies threaten their industries and jobs.

Xi said China will continue to invest in its industrial complex and ‌develop new technologies that would also benefit other countries. The world's second-largest economy will lower tariffs and further open up its markets, while standing up against protectionism and unilateralism, he added.

His "message is likely to resonate with many Global South countries and reinforces Beijing's effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group.

items: How China is positioning itself as a global leader as it hosts Trump, Putin
Ukraine cripples Crimean bridge in blow to Putin before meeting with Xi, Trump

blocks.text: Trump's trip to Asia is his first since his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections, while allegations involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy ​add to the tension.

Trump has downplayed the allegations, having developed a close relationship with Huang over the past two years, and both he and his Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have faced questions over when they knew about the allegations, given weighty decisions that were made by the White House over export controls on Nvidia chips.

items: No plans to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia chair tells investors
What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration

blocks.text: Most analysts expect Washington and Beijing to keep ties relatively stable as Trump and Xi are set to follow their meeting in Shenzhen with their fourth of the year at the Group of 20 gathering in Miami in December.

Putin, who was speaking after ⁠Ukraine crippled the vital Kerch road bridge linking Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war, followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as "former hegemons."
U.S. President Donald Trump and Xi applaud as the U.S. leader arrives at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Wednesday. (Mandel Ngan/Getty Images)
He said Europe ⁠was in a "humiliating decline" and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired.
"Experience has shown that the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their ⁠course, having lost much ⁠of their intimidating power," Putin said.
"While sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions ​may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth — let alone crushing the economies of competitors."
Ukraine's strike on Putin's bridge carries symbolic weight. Will it change the war?
Putin described the world as "turbulent" but said disagreements can be addressed by "sitting at the table."
"I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting," he said.
On Tuesday, Taiwan and Japan flagged incursions by Russian aircraft into their airspace.
In a bilateral meeting later, Xi and Putin praised their close partnership and pledged more measures that advance ​a "multipolar world."

In Manila, Trump vowed to deepen defence co-operation ⁠with the Philippines, amid its growing friction with Beijing over disputed features in the South China Sea. Earlier, he floated the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, but that has not been confirmed.
With files from CBC News

'Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,' House Speaker Bojie Dy tells ASEAN parliamentarians

items: The ASEAN parliamentary body is increasingly concerned about the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and the need for a collaborative regional approach to address its challenges.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The persistent threat of artificial intelligence (AI) is a cloud hanging over the parliamentary body of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but uncertainty remains over any concrete measure to approach the subject.

“It’s a concern for everybody, it’s a growing concern, and I think it cannot be addressed by one country. It has to be a concerted effort among the regions and other countries to be able to make sure that this is not abused,” House Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez, head of the Philippine delegation for the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly, said on the sidelines of the AIPA on Wednesday, November 18.

“Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,” House Speaker Bojie Dy, current AIPA president, also said in his opening speech.
Hernandez, however, sidestepped questions about whether a resolution on AI was being drafted during the AIPA general assembly, but said any effort will be “patterned on what transpired in the ASEAN.”

In 2025, the ASEAN adopted a declaration in Kuala Lumpur establishing an ASEAN AI Safety Network, a regional mechanism aimed at promoting collaboration among member states and addressing cross-border AI risks.

AIPA, as a regional parliamentary bloc, is not as powerful as the European Parliament. Any resolution passed during the general assembly is non-binding, which means it cannot force member parliaments to pass legislation back home.
AIPA, however, can still exercise influence by encouraging member parliaments to adopt regional commitments in their own countries.

Concerns about AI come as the Philippines’ hosting of ASEAN was met with massive protests against the US-led initiative Pax Silica, which will lead to the construction of a 1600-hectare AI industrial hub in New Clark City. The project is feared to displace hundreds of indigenous peoples and farmers, according to Human Rights Watch.
Only Singapore and the Philippines are ASEAN signatories to the Pax Silica initiative so far. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us
articles.summary: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

blocks.text: What happens when the people you inherited a business with are also the people you can no longer work with? You can quit a job, sell your shares, or find a new business partner. But what if that partner is your brother, sister, cousin, or parent, and the company is something your grandparents spent their lives building?

I have covered Philippine business families for most of my journalism career, interviewing relatives locked in battles over ownership, leadership, inheritance, and family land. Some disputes were already playing out in court, while others were waged quietly behind closed boardroom doors even as the companies kept running. As the feud between cousins Federico “Piki” Lopez and Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III unfolded this year, I found myself returning to those stories, my interview notes, and reading Harvard Business Review research on why family businesses fight and how some survive. In June, I joined family-business adviser Enrique Soriano in an online forum with business owners across Asia to discuss why even wildly successful dynasties break apart.

The Lopez cousins are hardly the first wealthy family to face this problem. India’s Ambani brothers split up the Reliance empire their father built, while the Ortigases fought over control of their real estate business. In Singapore, a father accused his son of trying to take over the board of one of the country’s biggest property developers. Some families eventually called a truce. Others decided they could no longer be business partners, and still fought for years, burning through cash on lawyers and leaving the next generation to clean up the mess.
All of this brought me back to one big question: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

For decades, the Lopez name has been tied to some of the Philippines’ most famous companies: ABS-CBN, Meralco, Benpres (now Lopez Holdings), First Philippine Holdings, First Gen, and Rockwell Land. The businesses changed over time, yet the family stayed connected to an empire their elders built, lost, won back, and rebuilt.

Under Oscar Lopez‘s leadership, the family published Phoenix, a book about how they bounced back from hard times. Piki wanted a different symbol for the next chapter: not the phoenix, which rises again after being destroyed, but the butterfly, which transforms into something completely new. He has also talked a lot about compounding, the idea that smart decisions made consistently over decades pay off far more than quick wins. In his September speeches to stockholders, he stressed that “direction matters more than speed,” pointing to the group’s decision ten years earlier to stop building coal-fired power plants even when coal was still making good money.

That mindset explains Piki’s game plan for First Gen’s energy investments. He believes the company must prepare for a power market that relies more and more on renewable energy. His cousins have questioned whether the bets he’s making are worth the massive price tag, risks, and years of waiting. They have also challenged his authority to make those calls on his own. Gabby and his allied cousins wanted something very different: immediate cash flow and shared family stewardship over a distressed media mission—ABS-CBN—that could not afford to wait until 2031 for long-gestation hydro projects to pay off.

blocks.caption: EXCLUSIVE: Inside Piki Lopez’s town hall as cousins rally for ABS-CBN

blocks.text: The fight turned public and personal. In April, majority owners of Lopez Inc.—representing three of the four branches of the family—accused Piki of acting “like a king without accountability,” questioning First Gen’s deals with Enrique Razon Jr.’s Prime Infrastructure, including selling control of its natural-gas business and investing in water-pumping hydropower projects. The majority group later called the hydropower bet “a horrible deal.” First Gen pushed back on those claims, defending the business logic, pricing, and board approvals behind its deals.

The cousins reached a ceasefire in May, but it didn’t hold, and by August, Gabby’s branch sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc., the private holding company sitting at the very top of the family empire, to businessman Ramon Ang for about P11.56 billion. Meanwhile, ABS-CBN lined up fresh funding. Piki then locked down control of the boards of Lopez Holdings and First Philippine Holdings (FPH), the two companies that hold the group’s stakes in First Gen and geothermal giant Energy Development Corporation (EDC). In November, FPH approved the proposed P15.92-billion sale of its 90.74% controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Gabby’s branch’s investment firm, Crème Investment Corporation, a deal that is still waiting to close. (READ: What it took to save ABS-CBN)
Taken together, these deals suggest the cousins are moving toward a future where they no longer have to agree on how to run the same businesses.
But is splitting up actually better than staying together?

One family owner wants bigger cash payouts today, while the relative running the company wants to plow back those profits into growing the business. Another thinks they should sell the company while buyers are offering a good price, while someone else wants to save it for the grandkids. One wants to ride out an industry slump, convinced a struggling business will bounce back, while another wants to stop pouring money into what looks like a sinking ship, especially when that cash could fund a different business that takes years of heavy spending before turning a profit.

Yet each walks away believing the others are greedy, reckless, or unreasonable. The real trouble starts when the people around the boardroom table aren’t just ordinary investors, but siblings who grew up competing for their parents’ and uncles’ attention, cousins who feel their branch of the family sacrificed more, or heirs who remember the founder’s wishes differently.

Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer, who advise business families and write for Harvard Business Review, explain how everyday business arguments turn deeply personal. In Why Fights Erupt in Family Businesses, they show how fights over money, power, and status get tangled up with family history. An argument over company spending can bring back old resentment over unequal treatment. A fight over who gets to be CEO can reopen old arguments about favoritism. Selling a company might look like a smart opportunity to one relative and a betrayal of the family legacy to another.

Soriano raised another complication during our webinar: many family businesses stay united for decades simply because one strong founder or family elder can settle all the arguments. Relatives might not like every decision, yet they accept the leader’s authority. Once that leader passes away, the next generation realizes it has inherited not only the businesses, but also old disagreements that were never truly resolved.

The Lopezes had larger-than-life leaders in Eugenio “Geny” Lopez Jr. and his brother Oscar, who died in 1999 and 2023, leaving their successors to figure out how to own and run surviving empires without those strong elders around to settle arguments.
Other Philippine families have ended up in far messier wars.

Take Banco Filipino, once the country’s biggest savings bank, famous for its slogan, “Subok na Matibay, Subok na Matatag (Tested Strong, Proven Stable).” Founded by Tomas Aguirre in 1964, the bank was shut down by the Central Bank in January 1985 before reopening in 1994 after the Supreme Court ruled the Central Bank had abused its power. But its headaches were far from over. It kept clashing with regulators over financial aid, its money troubles, and the fallout from its first shutdown.

blocks.caption: BANCO FILIPINO. This spread in Newsbreak’s March 3, 2003 issue shows the late Don Tomas Aguirre (left) and his children, Ana Marie Aguirre-Koruga (upper right), and Albert “Bobby” Aguirre (bottom right) on a polo field. Rappler

blocks.text: At the same time, the Aguirre family was tearing itself apart from the inside. I covered the legal fight involving Ana Maria Aguirre-Koruga, a minority stockholder who sued the bank’s directors in 2003, including her own brother, Albert Aguirre, who was then vice chairman. She accused them of risky banking practices, conflicts of interest, and shady loans meant to enrich insiders. The directors denied the claims. In 2009, the Supreme Court ruled in Koruga v. Arcenas that her complaints belonged with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), not a regular trial court. That ruling only decided who had authority to hear the case, not whether her accusations were true. The bank shut down for good on March 17, 2011, under BSP orders. The state deposit insurer, Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation, took over a bank with 62 branches, 173,480 accounts, and P17.8 billion in customer deposits. The family and regulators kept arguing over who was to blame. While the sibling feud wasn’t the sole reason Banco Filipino collapsed—its financial and regulatory problems ran much deeper—the family war played out inside a bank holding the life savings of thousands of ordinary Filipinos.

The Ilusorio family feud got even more personal. Potenciano “Nanoy” Ilusorio built a multi-billion-peso empire anchored by prime real estate, the pioneering satellite firm Philcomsat, and the exclusive Baguio Country Club. But by 1999, his six children had split into rival camps over their parents, the family fortune, and who should be in charge. When Nanoy grew old and frail, some of his children took him under their care, prompting their mother, Erlinda Kalaw-Ilusorio, to sue them for allegedly keeping her husband away from her, a battle the Supreme Court dismissed in 2001 as the “sad tale of a prominent family shattered by conflicts on expectancy in fabled fortune.” (READ: What drives people to declare war against their own flesh and blood?)

Even Nanoy’s death in June that year didn’t stop nearly 300 civil and criminal lawsuits filed between the rival camps, and according to an account Soriano published in 2016, some children only found out of Erlinda’s death four days later, leading to separate funerals. At one service, the urn reportedly held Nanoy’s ashes because another branch of the family kept Erlinda’s. Another service reportedly barred three of the sisters at the door with security guards.
A fight that started over money and power had reached the point where children could not even mourn their parents together.

In other prominent Philippine clans, the fracture began not at a parent’s deathbed, but when siblings began questioning how a brother or sister was managing inherited assets—turning boardroom suspicions into criminal complaints and proxy wars.

For the Jacintos, who built their wealth in steel, banking, and real estate, also fought over their inheritance. After their patriarch, Fernando Jacinto died, his children clashed over how family properties were being managed and sold. Musician and businessman Ramon “RJ” Jacinto stepped in after relatives questioned real estate deals handled by their sister Marilene, who was running parts of the family business. One fight centered on a large property in Misamis Oriental sold in 2007 for P226 million, which RJ’s camp argued was far below its appraised value. Another involved a Novaliches property reportedly worth about P300 million. Acting as president of family-owned Oregon Land Inc., RJ accused Marilene of faking a deed to transfer the land. Prosecutors charged her in 2012 with falsifying public documents, an accusation that led to criminal proceedings, though not a conviction. The feud showed how inheritance fights can quickly spiral into claims of betrayal and criminal charges between brothers and sisters. (READ: Shaping the future: Family legacies)

blocks.caption: Family feud: Court ruling saves Olivia Yanson’s share in PH’s biggest transport fleet

blocks.text: In the Yanson family, the trigger was a boardroom ouster over who would run the business. They parents founded Vallacar Transit Inc. and the Ceres bus empire, considered among the largest bus conglomerates in Southeast Asia with about 5,000 buses ferrying 700,000 to 850,000 passengers in routes across Visayas and Mindanao regions. In July 2019, four siblings—Roy, Emily, Ricardo Jr., and Ma. Lourdes Celina Yanson-Lopez—tried to oust their youngest brother, Leo Rey Yanson, from running the bus group. Their mother, Olivia Yanson, sided with Leo Rey and Ginette, splitting the family into Yanson 4 and Yanson 2 camps. They fought over who had the right to elect board directors and run the company, triggering lawsuits and battles over company records. In 2025, the Supreme Court said Olivia was mentally sound when she executed her will that designated the Yanson 2 camp as the righful heirs of their family business empire. The family still hasn’t reached the kind of broad peace deal needed to put the feud behind them. (READ: Yanson family feud gets uglier as court brands 4 siblings ‘fugitives from justice’)

This family drama resonated elsewhere in Asia where South Korea’s Lotte Group—the retail, hospitality, and confectionery giant behind Asia’s largest department stores, luxury hotels, and iconic snacks—became the stage for a succession war between brothers Shin Dong-joo and Shin Dong-bin, sons of founder Shin Kyuk-ho. The business giant had major operations in both Japan and South Korea. Dong-joo, the older brother, was prominent in Japan, while Dong-bin ran much of the Korean side. After Dong-joo lost top posts in Japan in late 2014 and early 2015, the brothers erupted into a public war over who had their father’s blessing and who should lead the empire. Their elderly father was pulled straight into the crossfire. At one point, Shin Kyuk-ho backed his eldest son, prompting Dong-bin’s camp to question whether their father was still mentally fit to make decisions. The brothers battled through shareholder votes, lawsuits, and press statements, turning their father’s mental health and legal guardianship into a court case. Dong-bin eventually won over shareholders and kept control, though Dong-joo kept fighting him. Instead of splitting the empire in two, one brother walked away with control of the main group.

blocks.caption: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

blocks.text: The Shin feud proved a hard truth: being the founder’s son, even being the oldest, doesn’t guarantee inheriting the throne.

In Singapore, the Kwek family— the powers behind iconic skyscrapers, luxury condos, and over 160 hotels worldwide—showed how quickly a disagreement between a father and son could move from the family boardroom into the headlines. In February 2025, City Developments executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng accused his son, chief executive Sherman Kwek, of attempting a boardroom “coup” by bypassing governance rules to appoint independent directors, prompting the elder Kwek to go to court to fire his son. Trading in City Developments shares was suspended as the confrontation became public. For a listed property developer, the dispute raised questions that went beyond the relationship between father and son: Who had the authority to appoint directors? Were corporate procedures being followed? And could the company continue operating effectively while its chairman and chief executive were fighting?

Yet the confrontation ended relatively quickly. On March 12, 2025, City Developments announced that the court proceedings had been settled and would be discontinued. Kwek Leng Beng remained executive chairman and Sherman remained chief executive, while the two newly appointed independent directors whose appointments had sparked the dispute, Jennifer Duong Young and Wong Su-Yen, stepped down. Singapore’s Straits Times later reported that trusted family friends and senior figures had helped mediate the truce. The company continued under the same family leadership, although the settlement did not necessarily mean that every personal disagreement had been resolved.

Here in the Philippines, the Ortigas family—the landed dynasty behind Ortigas Center and Greenhills—also managed to save its core property business after years of infighting. At stake was OCLP Holdings, which controls prime Ortigas land, Greenhills Shopping Center, and Tiendesitas. To gain an edge, rival branches teamed up with competing giants: the Rafael Ortigas group with Ayala Land, and the Francisco Ortigas group with SM Prime Holdings. The battle spilled into court over board elections and whether nominees tied to a rival developer could hold seats.

Those divisions let Ayala and SM deepen their footholds in a fractured enterprise. In November 2014, the developers and Ortigas factions dropped their lawsuits and agreed to work together. The family kept its landholdings intact rather than carving them up, though peace came at a steep price: bringing in powerful giants handed outsiders major influence over an empire that had belonged to the Ortigas family for generations.

There are strong business reasons to keep a family group intact. Companies under common ownership can share cash, talent, bank relationships, and leadership, allowing a stronger sister company to help a struggling one survive a rough patch or undertake massive investments too large for one branch alone. There is also the pull of family history, where a business built by a grandfather means far more to his grandkids than an ordinary stock investment, making a sale feel like erasing part of the family identity even when the financial math makes sense.
Yet keeping a company together merely because the founder wanted it kept together can create another problem: What happens when the next generation no longer agrees on what the business should do?

Adviser Josh Baron has argued in Why Family Businesses Need to Find the Right Level of Conflict that avoiding disagreement is actually unhealthy. Families must debate tough questions rather than letting owners quietly stew over decisions they feel powerless to change. When relatives can still negotiate and compromise, staying together preserves huge value. But when every investment, dividend payout, job appointment, or asset sale becomes another war for control, the cost becomes far too high.
India’s Ambani family decided that the brothers were simply better off running different companies. (READ: Timeline: Key dates in India’s Ambani brothers’ dispute)

After founder Dhirubhai Ambani died in 2002 without leaving a will, his sons Mukesh and Anil fought publicly over who would control Reliance Industries—India’s largest private-sector conglomerate, spanning petrochemicals, refining, telecom, and retail—until their mother, Kokilaben, stepped in to broker a June 2005 peace deal. Mukesh kept Reliance Industries and its core oil and chemical operations, while Anil took charge of telecom, power, and financial services. But it didn’t stop every argument as the brothers later fought over natural-gas supply deals in a battle that reached India’s Supreme Court. Still, they no longer had to agree on every single investment or management call.

India’s Bajaj family—one of the country’s oldest business dynasties, famous for putting India on wheels as a motorcycle, scooter, and financial services powerhouse—also split up its companies among different branches after years of fighting. Under a 2008 settlement, Shishir Bajaj’s branch took control of businesses like Bajaj Hindusthan and Bajaj Consumer Care, while other family branches kept the group’s core auto, finance, and industrial companies.

blocks.caption: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

blocks.text: Splitting up let each branch follow its own game plan. Their paths quickly diverged: the core Bajaj businesses boomed, while Bajaj Hindusthan struggled with heavy debt and a tough sugar market. Dividing the empire ended the fight over who was in charge, but it didn’t guarantee that both sides would win.

In Hong Kong, Walter Kwok was pushed out as leader of Sun Hung Kai Properties—the real estate titan behind the city’s tallest skyscrapers, luxury malls, and housing estates—in 2008 after clashing with his brothers Thomas and Raymond over how to run the empire. The battle pulled in their mother, Kwong Siu-hing, and tangled up the family trusts. Walter lost his executive job, though he didn’t lose his financial slice of the family fortune. He went on to start his own property company, Empire Group Holdings, while new trust rules spelled out each brother’s share of the family wealth.

Taking a different path is the Murdoch family—the real-life inspiration behind HBO’s hit drama Succession, and the media dynasty behind Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, and major outlets across the US, UK, and Australia that have shaped elections and public debate for decades. After a court battle over the family trust controlling voting power in Fox Corporation and News Corp, a September 2025 settlement locked in Lachlan Murdoch’s future control. His three older siblings from 95-year-old Rupert Murdoch‘s first two marriages—Prudence MacLeod, Elisabeth Murdoch, and James Murdoch—walked away with huge payouts and exited the trust. Grace and Chloe, Murdoch’s two youngest daughters from his third wife, Wendi Deng, stayed on as financial beneficiaries under the new setup, but without the voting power given to Lachlan.

Each of these families handled their split differently. The Ambanis and Bajajs divided up operating companies. Walter Kwok stepped out of management while keeping a financial stake. The Murdochs rewrote who holds voting control over their media empire. None of them offers a one-size-fits-all recipe for solving family feuds.

blocks.caption: ADVICE. Enrique Soriano, family business consultant of the Wong & Bernstein  Group, speaks during a forum. Courtesy of the Wong & Bernstein Group

blocks.text: Enrique Soriano, who has advised business families across the Philippines and Asia, does not view such separations as failures, noting during our June webinar that relatives who can no longer work together are often better served by an orderly division of business interests so they can stop being business partners without stopping being family.

Of course, that is much easier said than done. A family deciding to split still has to agree on who gets what, how much each company is worth, who takes on the debts, and what happens to shared properties. One relative might want out, only to find the others can’t afford to buy their shares. Another might want to keep control, but has to bring in an outside investor to help pay for the buyout.
And a peace deal that satisfies the relatives doesn’t automatically work out for the everyday public investors who also have money riding on those companies.

The Lopez cousins appear to be heading toward a more permanent split of their business interests, though whether that turns out well for their companies, outside stockholders, and the family itself will take years to see.
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN strugglesPart 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

Other business dynasties offer no easy answers: The Kweks and Ortigases found ways to keep their shared businesses intact after fierce battles, though both had to make major compromises. The Ambanis and Bajajs carved up their empires. The Kwoks and Murdochs separated day-to-day control from financial ownership. The Shin brothers’ succession war left one brother running Lotte, while the Aguirres, Ilusorios, Jacintos, and Yansons showed how family fights can spiral into years of lawsuits and lasting broken relationships and personal wounds.

There is a world of difference between keeping a company together because the owners actually agree on its future, and keeping it together just because nobody wants to be blamed for breaking up the family empire. There is also a difference between splitting up to chase new ambitions and splitting it up just to stop a fight.

For the Lopezes, going their separate ways may give each branch the freedom to focus on what it values most. Piki can concentrate on long-term energy bets, while Gabby and his allies can focus on lifestyle-related consumer and media businesses. Yet, that freedom brings new pressures, and success will depend on the choices each side makes next.

A family can survive a corporate divorce. Its companies might even grow stronger because of it. Or the split could leave both sides worse off than before. But the real question isn’t just whether relatives should stay together or go their separate ways. It is whether the businesses, and all the people who depend on them, will actually be better off afterward. – Rappler.com
Part 2 on Thursday, November 19 | Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?Part 3 on Friday, November 20 | Two cousins, two big bets: Will the Lopez split actually work?

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Apartment building collapses after explosion, fire in Glace Bay, N.S.
articles.summary: Cape Breton Regional Municipality say 17 people were reported injured in the early morning incident, and it's not clear yet if there were any fatalities.

image.caption: A fire has destroyed a building on Commercial Street in Glace Bay, N.S. (Submitted by Ernie Bagnell)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·Updated
Cape Breton Regional Municipality say 17 people were reported injured in the early morning incident, and it's not clear yet if there were any fatalities.
17 people reported injured in early morning incident in Cape Breton Regional Municipality
Crews from several fire departments in Cape Breton are on the scene of a building collapse and structure fire in Glace Bay, N.S., that injured 17 people.
The explosion happened around 6 a.m. on Wednesday at Pizza 67, a local pizzeria. The front of the building at 130 Commercial St. collapsed, said Cape Breton Regional Police.
The force of the explosion broke windows on nearby structures.
Shortly afterward, a fire started in the building, which has the pizza shop on the ground floor and about 20 apartments on the upper level.
Crews from more than a half-dozen fire departments responded to the incident. (Ernie Bagnell)
Cape Breton Regional Municipality spokesperson Christina Lamey said 17 people had minor injuries, and 14 of them were transported to Glace Bay Hospital.
Lamey said it is still unclear if there were any fatalities.
"The activity that's currently underway is to try to ascertain how many people were actually in the building," she said.
"We of course know of the 17 people that were assessed early in the morning but it will take some time to ascertain if everybody had made it out of the building."
A CBC reporter on the scene said most of the building has collapsed, and the structure was left with only one wall standing.
The explosion happened at 6 a.m. on Wednesday. (Ernie Bagnell)
Crews from seven or eight fire departments responded to the incident, as well as police and paramedics.

Ernie Bagnell, who lives in Glace Bay, was out early this morning grabbing a coffee when he spotted smoke downtown and drove to the scene. By that time, he said, the front of the building had collapsed.
"The firemen were there on top of it, up in the air, everywhere, trying to put it out, sirens in the distance," he said.
Lamey said as of 11 a.m., crews are still fighting the blaze, watering the site and an excavator is moving debris.
Crews working on a ladder truck fight the fire. (Ernie Bagnell)
The building is located near the intersection of Main Street and is next door to the Savoy Theatre.
Lamey said there are several street closures in the downtown area, and people are being asked to stay away from the area to allow emergency responders to do their work.
A comfort centre has opened at the Glace Bay Miners' Forum for building residents.
Lamey said it's too early to know what caused the explosion, collapse or fire.

articles.title: Corruption is in gov't DNA -- Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Corruption is in the government"s DNA Vice President Sara Duterte said in a social media post on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 7:20pm
Corruption is in the government’s DNA Vice President Sara Duterte said in a social media post on Wednesday.

In a Facebook post showing her attendance at the 52nd Philippine Business Conference and Expo ng Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PCCI) in October, Duterte said that Filipinos dream of a better future.
“Ngunit, malaking hamon sa pangarap na ito ang korapsyon na humahadlang sa atin sa pag-abot ng mas maraming oportunidad at sa kaunlaran,” Duterte said in the social media post.
(However, a big challenge to this dream is the corruption that blocks us from reaching more opportunities and progress.)
“It is a progressive disorder that has embedded itself deep within the DNA of the government—and tragically, it is the Filipino people who are left to suffer the consequences,” she added.
Duterte said as citizens, people should help each other reach that dream, adding that everyone had individual responsibilities.

“As citizens, we have responsibilities, too— to obey the law, reject corruption, protect our communities, participate in our democracy, and demand accountability from those who govern. Nation-building is a shared responsibility,” she said.

Duterte is currently the subject of an impeachment trial where she stands accused of having P817 million to P1.5 billion in unexplained wealth. She also allegedly failed to divest from businesses and did not declare her assets.

She and her defense team have denied all the charges against her. The Vice President has repeatedly cried foul on the corruption allegations, accusing the administration of political persecution. —Jean Mangaluz/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Over 200 ASEAN protesters ordered released from Camp Bagong Diwa
articles.summary: More than 200 protesters have been ordered released by the Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office following their arrest during a protest caravan amid the opening of the 49th Association of Southeast…

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published November 18, 2026 7:17pm
Supporters and advocacy groups gather outside Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City to decry the detention of over 200 ASEAN protesters on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. GMA News image

More than 200 protesters have been ordered released by the Muntinlupa City Prosecutor's Office following their arrest during a protest caravan amid the opening of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits in Pasay City.
According to a report Wednesday on GMA News' What We Know So Far, the Muntinlupa prosecutor's office issued the release order following the protesters' detention for the past three days.

The marchers have been held at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City after they were apprehended on Sunday, November 15, during a protest action slamming the planned US-led Pax Silica initiative and the presence of US President Donald Trump in the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit.
Activists and various sectoral groups have sounded the alarm over the potential risks of the Pax Silica project on the environment, as well as on the indigenous people it may displace.
The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) has already decried the mass detainment, noting that there were reports of minors being among those apprehended. Some protesters were also noticeably wounded.
The CHR also said that its lawyers and investigators were also initially denied access to the Muntinluipa protestors at Camp Bagong Diwa. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: NASA Voyager 1 probe believed to have reached ‘light-day’ milestone
articles.summary: Officials at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance

blocks.text: VOYAGER 1. An undated artist's concept shows NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft.
NASA/JPL-Caltech/Handout via Reuters
Officials at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance

items: NASA's Voyager 1 probe has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, approximately 16 billion miles, marking a significant milestone in space exploration.
Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object and continues to send back scientific data from interstellar space, including measurements of magnetic fields and cosmic rays.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, DC, USA – NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is believed to have now hit a distance milestone accomplished by no other spacecraft from Earth, based on advance computations by the US space agency, as the probe ventures through the near-emptiness of interstellar space.

The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 16 billion miles (26 billion km) — on Wednesday, November 18, at 5:16 am ET (1016 GMT).

Officials at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance. They have scheduled an event for Thursday, November 19, to discuss the milestone.
“Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see,” Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said.

Voyager 1, the most distant human-made object, is flying at almost 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kph). It crossed the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, to enter ‌interstellar space ⁠in 2012. Its twin, Voyager 2, was also launched in 1977 and entered interstellar space in 2018.
A Jet Propulsion Laboratory representative said recent power-saving measures could give the two Voyager spacecraft enough power to stay in communication with Earth for three to four more years.

“But the goal of the mission is to do science, and there is enough power to keep the current suite of instruments going through the 50th launch anniversary next year. Beyond that is hard to predict, and of course these are nearly 50-year-old spacecraft, and there are always things the team cannot anticipate that might happen,” the JPL representative said.

Voyager 1 journeyed past Jupiter and Saturn, the solar system’s two largest planets, earlier in its mission. It continues to gather scientific data. For instance, its instruments have detected the faint monotonous hum caused by the constant vibrations of the small amounts of gas present in interstellar space.

“Voyager is sending back continuous measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays and of plasma waves that we receive on Earth whenever the Deep Space Network points its antenna at Voyager,” Dodd said.
The Deep Space Network is NASA’s international array of giant radio antennas supporting interplanetary spacecraft missions.

“After the heliopause crossing, the magnetic field direction did not rotate into the interstellar direction as expected, but has maintained the direction it had when both Voyagers crossed the heliopause, a direction governed by our sun. We are watching to see when that rotation might occur,” Dodd said.

“We also are still observing effects from our sun, including strong solar storms like coronal mass ejections, that generate shocks and pressure fronts that reach as far away as Voyager 1 and beyond,” Dodd said. “Where does the sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Japanese PM visits Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae laid a wreath on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 7:16pm
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae laid a wreath on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City on Wednesday.
Takaichi is in the Philippines for the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, where she participated in several meetings with other world leaders.

“On November 18, commencing at 10:50 a.m. local time (11:50 a.m. Japan time), for approximately 10 minutes, Ms. Takaichi Sanae, Prime Minister of Japan, who is visiting the Philippines, visited the Heroes’ Cemetery and laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan said in a short statement.
According to the Armed Forces of the Philippines, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is dedicated to unidentified soldiers who died in the war.
It lies at the center of the Libingan ng mga Bayani with a simple plaque saying “Here lies a Filipino soldier whose name is known only to God.”
The statue serves as a monument where government officials and dignitaries would often conduct wreath-laying ceremonies.

“More than a monument, it stands as a solemn reminder of the countless Filipino soldiers whose identities may have been lost, but whose courage, sacrifice, and service to the nation will never be forgotten,” the AFP said in an X post in August.
During the Japanese occupation of the Philippines in World War II, thousands of Filipino soldiers and civilians were killed.
Japanese soldiers forced 70,000 to 76,000 Filipino and American soldiers to march 100 kilometers in what is now known as the Bataan Death March.
While historical accounts vary, thousands of soldiers died during the march due to hunger and exhaustion. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins
articles.summary: Cameron Bancroft claims the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.

blocks.text: Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.

In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian,, external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.
"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."
For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".
On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.
"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.
"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."
Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.
Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.
In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:

items: Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before Bancroft was caught
Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"
Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper
When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"
Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".

blocks.text: Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.
Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.
The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.
Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.
A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."
A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.
"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.
"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."
In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.
"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.
"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.
"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.
"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.
"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."

Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.
The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.
"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.
"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.
"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.
"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.
"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."

Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.
In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb.
"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.
"He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
"If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."
In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".
In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place.
"Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft.
"I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."
Analysis: Potentially the decisive intervention
For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.
But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.
Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.
His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.
In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.
Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.
It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.

But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.

Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.

What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?
Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.
Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.
