articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a spectacular, cynical and sometimes shallow joyride through the American psyche
articles.summary: Beyond an impossibly lavish presentation, the latest Grand Theft Auto game is mostly a familiar formula with some smart additions — and for the vast majority of players, it's exactly what they've…

image.caption: Lucia and Jason are the two playable characters in Grand Theft Auto VI, out Thursday on the Sony PlayStation 5 and Microsoft Xbox Series X&S consoles. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: For years, Grand Theft Auto VI has been many things: a meme for how long fans have been waiting for a new GTA title; a billion-dollar release; a potential spike in vacation and "sick" days; a talking point for unionization and workers' rights; a ticking cultural time bomb.
This week, finally, it's also ... a video game.

I've spent nearly 70 hours so far in GTAVI speeding across Leonida, the satirical version of Florida built by U.S.-based Rockstar Games (published by Take-Two Interactive). I've been following the story of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a young couple caught in a web of crime and conspiracies.

After dozens of robberies and car chases, it feels like I've only scratched the surface. But it doesn't take too long to learn that beyond an impossibly lavish presentation, this is mostly a familiar formula with some smart additions — and for the vast majority of players, it's exactly what they've been waiting for.
What's the story?

We first meet our dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, in a flashback: after a chance meeting at a carjacking, they flee the police and quickly fall in love. Flash forward and Lucia, in a moment of desperation, gets arrested after trying to rob a payday loans store.
Then we get the biggest surprise that previews have not hinted at: Jason and Lucia have a newborn boy named Tomas.

An animated gif shows the jumbo screens at Sankofa Square in Toronto displaying ads for Grand Theft Auto VI on Monday, and pedestrians walking near the EB Games store advertising the latest instalment in the video game series that launches worldwide on Thursday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Some months after her arrest, Lucia gets out (an early release program, thanks to an overcrowded carceral state). She reconnects with Jason, and the two quickly go back to a life of crime with the ultimate goal of saving enough cash to live crime-free with their son, who is currently in Lucia's aunt's custody.

Jason and Lucia are the most convincingly realistic protagonists of the series, with sympathetic aspirations and struggles with relatable trauma, coupled with a cavalier criminal charisma and simmering chemistry that sells the fact that this is, above all, a love story.
Grand Theft Auto VI wears its crime movie influences on its sleeve. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

The same can't be said for most of the game's supporting cast. It's a parade of one-dimensional racial or regional stereotypes, nearly all of them contemptible by design: twitchy drug runners, gun-toting rap moguls and lecherous lawyers.
These types of unbelievable caricatures stick out more when placed next to the believable Jason and Lucia.
How does it look?
The word that keeps coming to mind about GTAVI's world is "astonishing."
The near-photorealistic Vice City feels like a living, breathing city, and it's surrounded by ocean beaches, swamplands and suburbs, along with a full-sized international airport terminal.
Public art adorns sections of Vice City in Grand Theft Auto VI, while the city streets are packed with drivers and citizens. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Convenience stores feature barred windows and fading posters. Suburban lawns are frayed and worn where they meet the roads. The concrete that makes up the massive freeway networks is mottled and cracked.

You'll see non-player characters walking or sitting while having semi-realistic background conversations. Ocean Beach is packed with sunbathers of all body types, while the Jack of Hearts strip club is filled shoulder-to-shoulder with rowdy patrons and twerking models.

items: Grand Theft Auto VI nominated for game of the year, even though it isn't out yet
Vancouver duo's song goes viral after featuring in Grand Theft Auto VI

blocks.text: How does it play?

GTAVI's critical missions play out like a major scene in a modern summer blockbuster movie: breathtaking action and a dozen things happening (or exploding) at once. Screen wipes will zip you between Jason and Lucia's points of view as a heist goes wrong or a gang war erupts.
Unfortunately, they're also the least engaging for the player.

As Lucia struggles with a mercenary in a stairwell in a scene ripped from a John Wick movie, you'll do little more than mash the square button to get out of a chokehold. Jason might fend off a dozen armed goons, but it'll only last a few seconds before you're whisked away to another scene.
PHOTOS | Grand Theft Auto VI ads hit the streets:
It feels more like you're strapped into an amusement park ride than an active participant, as the game desperately tries to prove that it's cool. (To be fair, it is very cool.)
Peel away the bombast and you'll find GTAVI's true strength in its conventional core: stealing cars, robbing stores and banks, and losing the cops.

Every stick-up could follow the same rough outline: flash your guns at the store clerks, intimidate security out of trying to shoot you down, before smashing and grabbing cash, jewelry and more, and getting the heck out of there as quickly as possible.

But there's always a tension with every new location: How many guards are there? Will someone on-site know the safe code, where the good stuff is? Will a jittery customer try to wrestle you down? Are the police too far away to respond, or just around the corner?
Players will make most of their money by stealing it, whether from banks, corner stores or hideouts. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
This is an open-world game, though, and familiar technical frustrations frequently show up.

Shooting and fisticuffs are competent, but clunky. Your AI-controlled companion might choose to slowly saunter to your getaway vehicle instead of jumping in, giving the cops precious few seconds to swarm you. Inventory management quickly becomes a mess, as you try to keep track of which guns Jason or Lucia are holding.

Speeding from the police or gang members can get hairy, with most cars swerving or spinning out more quickly than you might expect, until you shell out for high-end street racers or all-terrain vehicles.

items: Is Grand Theft Auto VI the most anticipated video game of all time? Here are some reasons why
Grand Theft Auto 6 leak generates massive hype, and backlash

blocks.text: Do I really need to buy gas for my car?
Yes, but it's only an occasional pit stop. Much has been said of the other life simulation aspects that have been added to the game.

Nearly every possible interaction will have an effect on Jason and Lucia's stats. Working out at the gym keeps their health and stamina up. Eat junk food and you'll gain weight; don't eat at all and hunger will slow your health regeneration. Even small actions like petting a cat will buff your focus meter (used to slow down time during gunfights).
Players will need to work out at the gym and eat (mostly) healthy foods to keep Jason and Lucia in peak health. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
It's a thoughtful system, but the actions aren't terribly engaging. Most gym activities simply ask you to mash or hold buttons at a certain pace, for example.

Taking the time to make Jason and Lucia hold hands, watch TV together or just give a kiss on the cheek will build their relationship meter. It's a neat bit of world-building, though ignoring it will do little to impede your journey.
How political does it get?

The GTA series has always been known for its biting satire on American culture, but even its creators have admitted the last decade's absurdities have made that more difficult, especially when things veer into the explicitly political.
To their credit, the writers walk close to that line.

A right-wing talk radio channel features a blowhard sports host who complains about trans women in sports and promises to "make sports great again." Left-wing-coded environmentalists attempt to free captive animals while spewing nonsense about energy crystals.
Tyrone, seated right, is one of your main contacts in Grand Theft Auto VI. He'll pay top dollar for stolen drugs you'll find in rival gangs' hideouts. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Every end of the spectrum appears to be fair game, but the end result feels like blanket nihilism. Everyone is either selfish, a liar, an idiot or all three. It's hard to find truly incisive humour when the only punchline is "man, that guy sucks."

The world is full of painfully obvious knock-off brands, nearly all of them sexual innuendos or fart jokes. (The finance app on your phone is called BuckMe; a popular lemon-lime soda is called Sprunk.)
Taken individually, most of these jokes are passable. Some dialogue is laugh-out-loud hilarious. Before long, though, it becomes exhausting.

Occasionally, missions veer into gritty and even chilling drama, often revolving around the gang wars in Vice City. In momentary flashes, they're as gripping as something from The Wire; but they're jarring when placed next to gags you'd find on Family Guy.

Raul Batista leads a crew of thieves and safecracking experts in Vice City. Jason and Lucia will work with his team in a series of high-stakes heist missions in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
Can kids play it?

GTAVI is rated M for Mature (ages 17 and older) by the Entertainment Software Rating Board. Its description is a full bingo card of offensive content: blood and gore, nudity, strong language, use of drugs and more.

Gunplay is graphic, with blood and bits flying with a good headshot, though it's nothing you won't see in a modern shooter or horror game. Sexual content oscillates from romantic love scenes to churlish BDSM gags. Every swear word you can think of gets generous representation.
It's not a game for kids, obviously. Parents of teenagers will know what they can handle, but might want to play together and talk about it along the way.
Grand Theft Auto VI features several locations and regions outside of the Miami-like Vice City, including smaller suburbs and towns, swamplands and forests. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
Should you play it?
Chances are you're among the millions of people who've already pre-ordered Grand Theft Auto VI.
So while the latest GTA won't change how designers think about open-world video games, it comes in such a lavish presentation and package most players won't care.
For them, it will be more than enough to sit back on the couch while driving down Leonida's freeways at night, with neon-soaked skyscrapers in the distance as classic '80s rock plays on the radio.

articles.title: Medicine Hat, Alta., seeks to become 'drone city' as defence dollars roll in
articles.summary: As Canada boosts its military spending, officials in Medicine Hat, Alta., are seeking out new investment and economic activity tied to new private sector engagement by the Canadian Forces at CFB…

image.caption: Models of unmanned aircraft sit on a display table during a conference on defence investment in southeastern Alberta on Oct. 29 in Medicine Hat. (Collin Gallant/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary

As Canada boosts its military spending, officials in Medicine Hat, Alta., are seeking out new investment and economic activity tied to new private sector engagement by the Canadian Forces at CFB Suffield.
Long known as 'Gas City,' southern Alberta community seeks new investment
It's half the size of Prince Edward Island under a wide prairie sky and could be a launch pad for economic development and diversification in southeast Alberta.

Local officials, the Canadian Forces and private defence contractors say Canadian Forces Base Suffield is a key piece to upgrade Canada's military and potentially bring high-tech drone testing, new defence spending and jobs to the region that is dominated now by ranching and oilpatch activity.

"I think that CFB Suffield is the secret weapon in the arsenal of tools that southeast Alberta has to grow in the defence industry," said Lt.-Col. Mike Onieu, a former base commander of the 2,700-square-kilometre firing range located about 50 kilometres west of Medicine Hat.

Now in charge of future projects at the base, Onieu told 220 delegates at a defence forum in Medicine Hat on Oct. 29 that his mission is to maximize the facility in light of a national strategy to boost domestic defence research and drone technology.
"Most importantly, we need to unlock the base for third-party uses," he told the audience, which included private sector defence contractors.
"We understand the incredible demand by industry and third parties to access the base. We haven't figured out how that's going to look yet, but it is going to happen."
Companies' desire to use the heavily restricted space — potentially bringing work crews and researchers, or potentially locating operations nearby — is what Medicine Hat is banking on.
City seeks new investment, new direction

Long known as the "Gas City," the city located 300 kilometres from Calgary is attempting to reinvent itself as the "Drone City" — a campaign to lure entrepreneurs, engineers and skilled high-tech trade workers from larger centres to work in the aerospace industry.

A commercial showcasing the community, its amenities, short commutes and lower housing costs debuted earlier this month during the national broadcasts of a recent curling event held at the city's 6,000-seat junior hockey arena.
Front and centre are drone companies already in the city, located to take advantage of Suffield's proximity.

"The companies that we have here now want to grow," Mayor Linnsie Clark told CBC News at the same city-sponsored defence conference. She sees the city's role in "workforce attraction" to "empower" that growth.
"[Then], naturally, some of their partners in the supply chain or [work] they're contracting out to other places now, will hopefully move to Medicine Hat.
"That is truly an integrated cluster."
Three major drone companies in the city already employ about 100 workers — notable in the city of 69,000 — but economic officials believe much more is possible.

The city, Medicine Hat College, several economic development groups and private industry are collaborating to create a "defence innovation hub." It seeks to remove barriers for high-tech firms and spur stagnant local economic and population growth.
Aerospace development is a key pillar of a four-year economic development plan of municipalities in the region.

"There's an appetite to attract new business, expand the current business," said Vincent Malley, head of business development for UVA Dynamics, a drone developer in Medicine Hat now competing for contracts in the recently announced European defence bank.
"Leveraging those assets that we have, it gives a foundation to be able to do that."

Lt.-Col. Mike Onieu is head of evaluating future projects at Canadian Forces Base Suffield, a huge military live-fire range near Medicine Hat that is now increasingly used for drone research. (Collin Gallant/CBC)
New investment in drones, research
Canada's military leaders have promised fast action to integrate drones into Canadian Forces and make procurement a faster and more efficient process for private industry.
The latest federal budget includes $2 billion over five years specific to drone capabilities as the overall defence budget grows.

items: LISTEN — Drone manufacturer reacts to federal budget defence spending commitments
Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence

blocks.text: The Defence Research and Development Canada facility at the base currently employs about 180 scientists and support workers.

The Forces operation at the base employs 220 employees, according to the Department of National Defence — about 200 less than when Canada supported annual British Army tank training exercises for up to 10,000 troops.
New drone-defence technology put to the test at Canadian showcase

The British military moved heavy armour training to Eastern Europe in 2023, but returned to Alberta this year for smaller drone-focused exercises. Two similar deployments for drone testing and anti-drone training are scheduled for 2027, said Onieu.
Canada also held a similar "Sandbox" exercise this fall — inviting contractors to test prototypes and receive feedback from military officials at an early stage of development.

Onieu said that sort of industry engagement will continue at Suffield as its size allows secure remote spaces to evaluate electronic signal-jamming technology and other anti-drone measures away from civilian populations.
Susan Rowsell, the chief scientist at Defence Research and Development Canada at Suffield, said the base's proving ground is large enough and secure enough to test military applications.
"You can't just go and do this in the soccer field or at the Medicine Hat airport," said Rowsell.
"There are certain things you just can't do outside of this area."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Collin Gallant is a journalist with the CBC's bureau in Medicine Hat, Alta., covering a wide array of topics in southeast Alberta. Reach him by email at collin.gallant@cbc.ca

articles.title: Axes and cutlasses: Violence on Nigeria's election campaign trail
articles.summary: As Nigeria's January 2027 polls inch closer, a spate of violence and political thuggery during campaign rallies and town hall meetings is raising concerns about the safety of citizens participating…

image.caption: There are growing concerns over rising political violence ahead of the January 16, 2027 electionImage: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Samuel Adebanjo had gone to the Oregun area of Lagos, the economic heartbeat of Nigeria, to cover a town hall meeting organized by the opposition party, the National Democratic Congress (NDC). But what was supposed to be a routine reporting assignment took a violent turn when a group of armed men stormed the venue and disrupted the gathering.

"I was at the entrance, taking photos of people entering the hall when some buses drove in and I heard a loud bang," Samuel recalled. Before he could process what was happening, the men began chasing supporters of the party with axes, cutlasses, and wooden planks, forcing many to flee for safety.

Adebanjo ran towards the parking lot, hoping to find somewhere to hide. But some of the attackers spotted him and gave chase. The journalist with the local newspaper, The Cable, was surrounded by five men who started hitting him to make him let go of his camera. Despite wearing a press jacket, they accused him of being the party's cameraman. "They wanted to collect the camera. I was struggling with them because I didn't want them to take it away. In the process, my middle finger was broken," he said.

During the struggle, one of the thugs raised his axe and struck it towards his wrist. "I used my hand to guard it. I was expecting blood. I never knew it landed on my wristwatch, and that's when it hit me that they're not joking, and that I had to let go of my equipment."

blocks.caption: Observers say political violence could deter some voters from coming out to cast their ballot on election dayImage: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: He was left in agonizing pain. By the time the violence subsided and he was taken to the hospital, he had sustained a broken middle finger and internal injuries around his ribs. The attack also left several other people injured and properties, including vehicles belonging to supporters of the party, destroyed.

As the January 16, 2027 general election inches closer, incidents like this are becoming increasingly common, as incumbent Bola Tinubu battles for re-election on a ticket that revolves around combating insecurity and resolving the country's biting economic crisis.
Election-related violence on the rise

Adebanjo's experience is not an isolated incident. According to the National Peace Committee, 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord have been recorded across the country's 26 states and the federal capital, Abuja.

Between August 19, when the campaign kicked off in the West African country, and October 27, political violence and thuggery, as well as misinformation and disinformation, top the violations, accounting for 33 and 29 incidents respectively.

Campaign rallies, town hall meetings and other political events organized by parties have been marred by violence, threats and intimidation, prompting analysts to caution that rising violence could taint the credibility of the elections and discourage voter participation.

On November 15, a group of men attacked the campaign convoy of former Kano state governor and National Democratic Congress vice-presidential candidate Rabiu Kwankwanso during a visit to the Bichi area of Kano. Similar incidents were recorded in both Sokoto and Kebbi when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar took his campaign to the northwestern states.

Civil society groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned the spate of election-related violence and intimidation across the country, urging security agencies to bring perpetrators to book. President Tinubu has also condemned the rising incidents of violence at political events, warning that intimidation and political thuggery capable of disrupting public order would not be tolerated.
Nigeria's history of electoral violence

Political violence is not new to Nigeria; nearly all of the country's elections have been tainted by violence and intimidation, including the deadly post-election violence that followed the 2011 elections, where at least 800 people were killed over days of rioting in states across northern Nigeria.

Raheem Mutiu, a Nigerian researcher at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global organization that collects data on conflicts and political violence worldwide, told DW that the pattern ahead of the coming polls is shaping up to show "political groups more agitated and determined to win elections by all means."

Mutiu described the spate of violence since the campaign was flagged off as mind-boggling. "Within the period of two months, we have recorded over 30 politically linked attacks with 10 fatalities. But what this one points to is that politically linked attacks have become more frequent and geographically widespread ahead of the January 2027 general election," he said.
Peter Obi: 'I will not lose' — but can he deliver?

The country's multiparty politics has entrenched a winner-takes-all system that fuels fierce competition among parties and, at times, a willingness to resort to violence. There's also a growing intolerance for opposition among party supporters, although perpetrators are difficult to identify because they often act anonymously and as proxies for the interests they support.

"What we have seen again is that supporters across the political spectrum are involved in the attacks, but intensity of their violence and engagement largely depends on their local stronghold and territorial dominance," Mutiu added.
The high cost of violence

A voter choosing under threat is not choosing freely, Dengiyefa Angalapu, a researcher at the Abuja-based Center for Democracy and Development, told DW. He noted that apart from the physical attacks, the spread of fake news and hate speech narratives, which form part of the non-physical breaches of the peace accord, "can deceive voters and undermine trust in genuine information."

blocks.caption: The 2023 election saw the lowest voter turnout since Nigeria returned to democracy in 199Image: Sunday Alamba/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Angalapu stressed that the growing threat of electoral violence could further undermine voter participation in a country already struggling with low turnout. More than 103 million Nigerians are registered to vote in the 2027 general elections, according to the country's electoral authority.

However, the country has consistently recorded low voter participation, with the 2023 general elections witnessing the lowest turnout since Nigeria's return to democratic rule in 1999. Only 27% of the nearly 94 million registered voters cast their ballots.
"Intimidation adds another pressure: someone who fears punishment for their political preference may avoid meetings or withdraw from politics altogether," Angalapu added.

Adebanjo is still recovering from his injuries. The attack has left him with a bigger question about safety ahead of the polls: "If this could happen to me, a journalist, how much more to the citizens? I am not sure, at this stage, people will even come out to vote."

articles.title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
articles.summary: Thursday's meeting between the leaders of US, China and Russia will give Vladimir Putin a big stage - but it does not bring him closer to winning the war in Ukraine.

blocks.text: The meeting hasn't even happened yet.
But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.
Whatever the outcome.
Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.

Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.
That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.
It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.

"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.
That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.
But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.

It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.
One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.
In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."
But what of those who are not at the table?
Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.

Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.

Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.
"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.

It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".
In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.
Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.
Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.
The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.
It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.
The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.
It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

articles.title: Latin America's mega-prisons: Can El Salvador's model work?
articles.summary: El Salvador's mega-prison has become a model for governments across Latin America seeking to combat organized crime. But experts question whether the approach is effective, sustainable or compatible…

image.caption: Inside El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT). Image released by the El Salvador presidential press office following its inauguration in 2023Image: Press Secretary Of The Presidency Of El Salvador/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Around 15,000 inmates and a capacity of up to 40,000, prison sentences of up to 1,000 years, strict security measures and an extreme isolation regime. Staged images show inmates with shaved heads and tattoos being subdued by heavily armed guards.

These are just some of the facts circulating about El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), a symbol of President Nayib Bukele's security policy and a possible model for other Latin American countries seeking to combat organized crime.

More than a dozen governments in the region have proposed building similar "mega-prisons," although most would have a far smaller capacity. A range of experts consulted by DW question the effectiveness and sustainability of these initiatives.
What is a mega-prison?

De facto mega-prisons — that is, overcrowded prisons with excessive inmate populations — existed in Latin America long before Bukele, says criminologist Jose Luis Perez Guadalupe, former president of the National Penitentiary Institute and former interior minister in Peru. Lurigancho Prison in Lima, for example, designed to hold 3,000 inmates, has housed nearly 11,000 for decades.

But ever since CECOT was launched in 2023, the concept of a "mega-prison" has been primarily linked to maximum-security facilities. For Olga Espinoza, an academic specializing in prison systems at the School of Government of the University of Chile, this association is problematic because it implies that the entire prison population requires "extremely severe" punishment.
High costs and a questionable track record

According to Espinoza, placing the entire prison population in maximum-security facilities would amount to inefficient and extremely costly "over-intervention." These facilities require substantial investments in infrastructure, technology, specialized staff, anti-corruption measures and social reintegration programs.

It would also be ineffective because "international evidence indicates that when people with different profiles are placed in the same space, there is a high risk of the spread of criminal behavior," the Chilean expert adds.

Several criminal groups across the region even have their roots in overcrowded prisons: Tren de Aragua in Venezuela; Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones in Ecuador; and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) in Brazil.

Even when the proposal involves simply building large-scale facilities, investing in a single structure may seem attractive given the difficulties of developing public infrastructure in Latin America.

However, "there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that building mega-prisons is more cost-effective," says Renato Rivera, a senior analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).

The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, adopted in 1955, "the recommendation has been to build medium-sized prisons housing between 1,000 and 2,000 inmates rather than mega-prisons," explains Perez Guadalupe, a professor at the Universidad del Pacifico in Lima.

"Mega-prisons, apart from being impersonal, can become extremely dangerous," says Guadalupe. As an example, the GI-TOC's Rivera highlights the widely reported prison massacres in Ecuador in 2021 that took place in the country's largest and most populated facilities.
Security, propaganda and human rights

Experts acknowledge that mass incarceration has coincided with a dramatic decline in violence in El Salvador and has strengthened the public's perception of safety. Despite reports of arbitrary arrests, abuses and more than 500 deaths in state custody in the country, announcements of new mega-prisons project an image of a strong state confronting organized crime across the region.

However, they warn that this political and symbolic impact does not guarantee sustainable results. Achieving them would require a "clear commitment" to external oversight, human rights protections and social reintegration programs, which governments have yet to demonstrate, Espinoza says.

Perez Guadalupe is particularly critical of the Salvadoran model, describing it as "pure propaganda." He believes the images released from CECOT violate human dignity. He also argues that the state must demonstrate "moral superiority over those who break the law."

blocks.caption: El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele's hardline approach has included mass arrests, a prolonged state of emergency and the construction of the country's massive CECOT prisonImage: Jose Cabezas/REUTERS

blocks.text: Can the Salvadoran model be exported?
Although transnational organized crime represents a growing challenge across the region, the Peruvian criminologist considers El Salvador's case exceptional.

Following the mass arrests carried out under the state of emergency introduced by Bukele, the country has one of the highest incarceration rates in the world. CECOT was designed to permanently detain members of gangs such as MS-13 and Barrio 18, which are considered extremely dangerous.

However, the reality of other Latin American prison systems is different. The question is not where to lock people deprived of their liberty away forever, but rather "how we want them to leave: worse or better," Perez Guadalupe argues, pointing out that most will eventually return to society.
What are the alternatives?

In theory, the official alternative is provided by the UN Nelson Mandela Rules for the treatment of prisoners, updated in 2015. They establish principles for modern prison management, including respect for human dignity, an absolute prohibition on torture and degrading treatment and social reintegration as a central goal of imprisonment.

In practice, Latin America has developed innovative approaches in this direction. These include the APAC model in Brazil, which operates facilities without guards, weapons or violence; Conflict Prevention and Resolution Committees in Argentina; and the Alternative Criminal Justice Center in the Mexican state of Sonora.
Experts also point to the need for maximum-security prisons for specific inmate profiles, but on a smaller scale and with more precise classification of the prison population.

Finally, they emphasize that prisons, including mega-prisons, primarily address the consequences of organized crime rather than its root causes. Poverty, social exclusion and a lack of opportunities require public policies focused on employment, education and social integration to reduce the conditions that enable crime to expand in one of the world's most unequal regions.
This article was originally published in Spanish.

articles.title: SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site unless ministers intervene
articles.summary:
Energy firm says existing market arrangements do not sustain facility’s continued operation

The energy company SSE has warned it will close its Atwick natural gas storage facility in…

blocks.text: The energy company SSE has warned it will close its Atwick natural gas storage facility in northern England next summer, if the government does not intervene to offer support amid weak market conditions.

The site, located near Hornsea on the East Yorkshire coast, consists of eight caverns with the capacity to store about 309m cubic metres of gas, estimated at about 1.5 days’ worth of Great Britain’s gas usage.
SSE said in an update to investors: “It is increasingly clear that existing market arrangements do not support their continued operation.”
It added that gas storage facilities such as Atwick have a “strategic importance” to the energy system.

Energy companies rely on stockpiling gas in their storage facilities during the summer, when demand is lower and prices are usually lower, before withdrawing the stored gas and selling it during winter when demand for energy for heating and power peaks.
However, the gas price increase triggered by the Iran conflict and the effective closure of the strait of Hormuz have made it uneconomical to stockpile gas during the summer.
As a result, countries across Europe have entered the cooler months of the year with gas stores at their lowest level in more than a decade.

SSE said: “Despite current commodity prices, favourable spreads are not emerging to support the ongoing commercial operation of Atwick.” It came as the company announced its results for the six months to the end of September.
The closure of a gas storage facility such as Atwick could leave the UK even more exposed to price shocks on global markets.
Britain already stores less gas than some of its European neighbours and is instead more reliant on liquefied natural gas imports.

SSE’s announcement comes months after British Gas’s owner, Centrica, warned it would close its Rough site – the UK’s largest gas storage facility – unless it can agree a long-term financial support deal with the government.
The trade union Unite has called on ministers and Centrica to work together to secure the future of Rough, which the company has scheduled for closure in April 2027.
after newsletter promotion
SSE said it continued to engage with the government “on the need for policy intervention to support a resilient gas system”.
The Atwick facility has been in operation since 1979 and has been owned by SSE since September 2002.

The jump in wholesale gas prices has fed through into household bills. On Wednesday the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast the typical household gas and electricity bill will jump by 26% in January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year.
The government has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Investing in AI Literacy Means Investing in Judgment
articles.summary: Knowing how to use an AI tool does not settle when to use it, what to trust it with, or
articles.byline: Angel Chiang, Jewel Zhu, Paolo Miguel Ordonio

blocks.text: Knowing how to use an AI tool does not settle when to use it, what to trust it with, or how it can serve other people. These questions are part of AI literacy, alongside an understanding of the technology itself. Helping people make such judgments requires education that connects AI with their circumstances and responsibilities.

For Break the Fake Movement in the Philippines, this work builds on its focus on media and information literacy and countering disinformation. In a March 2026 research interview with the Centre for Asian Philanthropy and Society (CAPS), co-author Paolo Miguel Ordonio, Break the Fake Movement’s executive director, explained that its AI education emphasizes foundational understanding and critical thinking, and its curriculum includes ethics, copyright, data privacy and safety. He described enthusiasm for AI that does not always translate into understanding, alongside communities where some learners still need help with basic digital activities.

Different audiences also bring different needs. At the time of that interview, Break the Fake Movement was exploring how to adapt its AI literacy training for civil society workers through a collaboration with the Association of Foundations. Modules developed primarily for young people, parents and educators provided a starting point; understanding what civil society workers needed from AI education was part of the adaptation.

For civil society workers, AI literacy needs to address decisions they face at work: which problems AI can help solve, which tasks it can support, and where human judgment should remain central. CAPS’s report, Cars Without Roads: Investing in AI for Good Across Asia, illustrates the kinds of decisions people may face. Organizations approaching Infoxchange with plans to adopt AI sometimes discover that they first need better data management, stronger cybersecurity or a clearer definition of the problem they want to solve. In a separate CAPS interview, Hyomi Ahn, a researcher at Korea’s Beautiful Foundation, described its work to develop internal AI guidelines. She also highlighted debate among advocacy organizations about whether AI should draft public statements, raising questions about which work should remain human.

AI literacy programs can be designed for staff and leaders alike, with learning adapted to their different responsibilities. Staff may need to judge how AI fits their tasks; leaders may need to learn how to set expectations, develop guidance and provide time and resources for staff learning. The report’s findings on organizational readiness suggest that this education should also help people recognize when specialist advice is needed and what support colleagues need to apply their learning.

Yet funding for literacy education can be difficult to secure. Drawing on Break the Fake Movement’s experience, Ordonio described limited funding opportunities for literacy education, saying that funding favored infrastructure, tools and systems. His experience reflects the report’s wider concern that human capability and supporting conditions receive less investment than visible applications. In the study’s pre-interview survey of 36 organizations, 72.2% of respondents identified training and capacity-building as underinvested, the highest share for any category and more than double that of any other area.

blocks.caption: Executive Ordonio delivering a lecture on AI usage for parents.

blocks.text: For funders, this means supporting AI literacy programs that adapt learning to participants’ responsibilities and provide opportunities to consider where AI fits their work, whose needs it serves and what responsibilities its use entails. Funding this learning recognizes informed judgment as a capability worth developing and an essential part of turning technological possibilities into social value.

articles.title: The new milestone Voyager 1 just crossed in interstellar space
articles.summary: Voyager 1, already the farthest a human-made object has ever gone, has crossed the arbitrary but important threshold of a light day. It now takes 24 hours to send a message to the probe, now in…

image.caption: This undated artist's concept depicts NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft entering interstellar space, or the space between stars. NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is officially the first human-made object to venture into interstellar space, according to a NASA statement. The 36-year-old probe is about 12 billio

blocks.text: Science

Voyager 1, already the farthest a human-made object has ever gone, has crossed the arbitrary but important threshold of a light day. It now takes 24 hours to send a message to the probe, now in interstellar space.
It took nearly 50 years to get to this point
It took nearly 50 years to get to where Voyager 1 is now. But it takes light just a day.
That's the new milestone — 16 billion miles, to be precise — the spacecraft has just reached.

“What it means is it takes a full day for light or radio signals from Earth to reach Voyager,” said Jason Rhodes, chief scientist for astrophysics, heliophysics and fundamental physics at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
“And it takes, of course, then another full day for the signals back from Voyager to reach Earth.”
It's not to scale, but Voyager 1 has come a long way in nearly 50 years. (CBC)

Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 was meant to study the gas giants of our solar system, Jupiter and Saturn. But by 1998, it continued on past them, becoming the farthest human-made object ever. It reached interstellar space — the region just outside the sun’s magnetic influence known as the heliopause — back in 2012, at a distance of 18 billion kilometres. Now, it’s more than 26 billion kilometres away.

“When we're talking about these scales, it really reminds us just how big space is,” said Bethany Downer, who works on the communications team for the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, “and how impressive it is that something relatively small that we constructed is able to keep going indefinitely that way.”

items: Are we alone? Institute searching for alien signals is using a new way to answer that age-old question
A spacewalk to remember: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says seeing Earth 'changed' him

blocks.text: Still working, talking

Arguably, being a “light day” away is an arbitrary threshold, as there’s no new physical boundary or change to Voyager 1 itself. But experts say it’s remarkable because it’s still plugging along on its mission while communicating with Earth.
LISTEN | Nearly 50 years later, Voyager 1 is still working:
Quirks and Quarks21:54EXTENDED EDITION: Voyager 1 on the edge of reaching historic one light-day milestone
“It's not operating, of course, as much as it used to be. There aren't as many instruments on board that are capturing science,” Downer said.

Voyager 1’s power is generated by the heat from the natural decay of plutonium. As that power has dwindled over nearly half a century, most of its science instruments have been shut down, the latest being the LCEP, which measured low-energy charged particles. There are two instruments that still work, one for measuring plasma waves and the other for magnetic fields.

“This tells us a lot about how stars form and how the distance between stars is not empty space, but filled with exciting particles and physics that we didn't really know about very well until Voyager,” Rhodes told CBC News from Pasadena, Calif.

Each of NASA's Voyager probes are equipped with three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), including the one shown here. The RTGs provide power for the spacecraft by converting the heat generated by the decay of plutonium-238 into electricity. (NASA/JPL-Caltech)

Those instruments communicate to Earth via the deep space network, antennas located at multiple sites around the world dedicated to keeping continuous communication with spacecraft. Though Voyager 1’s signals are faint, it’s clear there’s a pretty big message we want to hear.
“Most important thing is: 'I'm still turned on, I'm still operating,'" Downer told CBC News from St. John’s.
Going but never gone

NASA expects Voyager 1 (and its sibling Voyager 2, launched the same year but on a different path) to continue being able to send messages for another decade, but Rhodes says there’s no definite endpoint as teams continue to work on energy-saving measures to try and extend it.
But even powerless, their missions won’t be over.
The special payload onboard both Voyager spacecraft, containing a snapshot of life and culture on Earth. (NASA/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)
“Both have a golden record,” Rhodes said, “and it's made of gold because that's a metal that won't tarnish or rust or decay.”

Effectively a time capsule, the golden records capture a cross-section of sounds from humanity, from greetings in 55 different languages to music to natural sounds of the earth, including thunder and humpback whales.
If you’re wondering how anyone might know how to play it, there are instructions. If you’re wondering who might play it, well, they’d have to think a little like us.

items: Japan launches spacecraft to mysterious moons of Mars

blocks.text: They also contain a message in Morse code, said Downer: "Ad astra per aspera," or "To the stars, through hardships."

While the long road continues for Voyager 1, it’s already provided deep insights into our solar system. Not least of which, an insight into ourselves, from this image taken in 1990 by Voyager 1 from six billion kilometres away.
The Pale Blue Dot is a photograph of Earth taken Feb. 14, 1990, by NASA’s Voyager 1 at a distance of 3.7 billion miles (6 billion kilometers) from the Sun. (NASA/JPL-Caltech)

Known as the Pale Blue Dot, it shows Earth as a tiny speck, bathed in a beam of light. Taken at the request of American astronomer Carl Sagan, he immortalized the significance of being so insignificant in his book of the same name.
“Consider again that dot. That’s here. That’s home. That’s us.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Anand Ram is a reporter and producer with CBC's science and climate unit. He's worked as a reporter covering technology, business and the environment and as a producer with The National.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the South China Sea Code of Conduct?
articles.summary: The long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) has yet to be completed with Beijing and member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) unable to agree on several issues…

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 6:04pm

The long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) has yet to be completed with Beijing and member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) unable to agree on several issues — but what is it? And what is taking so long for the involved nations to agree?

While conflict in the South China Sea has had tense confrontations between China and the Philippines, parts of the contested waters have other claimants, including Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan, and Brunei.

According to the ASEAN's website, member state parties and Beijing agreed to issue the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) in 2002 to maintain peace in the disputed waters.

The agreement stated that all parties are seeking peaceful resolutions to their maritime disputes to ensure regional stability. In 2011, the Guidelines for the Implementation of the DOC was established, which further reinforced the declaration.

"The Parties concerned undertake to resolve their territorial and jurisdictional disputes by peaceful means, without resorting to the threat or use of force, through friendly consultations and negotiations by sovereign states directly concerned, in accordance with universally recognized principles of international law, including the 1982 UN (United Nations) Convention on the Law of the Sea," the DOC read, referring to the UNCLOS.

Also known as the Law of the Sea Treaty, the UNCLOS is the international agreement that defined the limits of the territorial seas of nations and the areas in which they could exploit marine resources. It also established the rules for the use of the high seas for international navigation, and outlined the rights and responsibilities of nations in the protection of the marine environment.

The UNCLOS served as a legal basis for the Philippines' case against China before an international tribunal in The Hague. The case was filed in 2013 and won in July 2016, junking China's nine-dash line claim over the South China Sea, but Beijing has been steadfast in refusing to recognize the ruling.
Years of negotiation

As for the DOC, the countries also agreed to practice self-restraint when conducting activities that could escalate disputes or affect stability, including occupying uninhabited islands, reefs and other features.

The DOC stated that the parties concerned reaffirmed "that the adoption of a code of conduct in the South China Sea would further promote peace and stability in the region and agree to work, on the basis of consensus, towards the eventual attainment of this objective."
It is this code that has taken years to negotiate.
According to the ASEAN website, discussions over the COC began in 2018 when the first draft was established. However, the undersigned countries have failed to reach an agreement.
Over the weekend, Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said the COC was about 80% finished, but salient issues remained.
She said the COC is likely to be finished in 2027. The DFA originally wanted to finish it by 2026, which would have coincided with the Philippines' chairship of the ASEAN.
Negotiations and China
While Lazaro did not dive into what the salient issues are, doubts have been raised about China's sincerity in establishing the COC.
The late former foreign affairs secretary Albert del Rosario said in 2014 that he doubted that China would work quickly for a legally binding COC.

"I'm not very optimistic about whether China is serious about an expeditious conclusion [of a Code of Conduct] because I can see the aggressive provocative acts that we are seeing now and which is, I think, is their way to pursue an expansion agenda," Del Rosario said.
The South China Sea, or the West Philippine Sea for areas within Manila's 200-km exclusive economic zone, has been a point of contention between Beijing and Manila for years.
Tensions have considerably risen during President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s term, with the present administration making a stronger claim over its maritime territories. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: [DECODED] Scam season and the leaks that may make it worse
articles.summary: If recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start

blocks.text: If recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start

items: With only 37 days until Christmas, holiday preparations are causing increased traffic in Metro Manila, coinciding with the recent ASEAN Summit.
A GSMA survey reveals that while many Filipinos are aware of scams, with 76% expressing concern, scams continue to evolve, including new methods like 'quishing' via QR codes.

Recent data breaches have exposed personal information from various government agencies, prompting warnings about increased scam risks during the holiday season and highlighting the need for better public awareness and reporting mechanisms.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

There are only 37 days before Christmas! Have you started your holiday preparations already, and are you feeling the Christmas rush yet? I’ve noticed that Metro Manila traffic has been heavier over the past week, although that may have been due to preparations for the 49th ASEAN Summit, which just wrapped up.

Between the traffic and the shopping, the holidays are when we’re busiest and least careful, especially with our transactions. A recent survey by the global industry trade organization GSM Association (GSMA) said that Filipinos do know the risk: 76% said they “absolutely worry” about scams and 78% said they changed their behavior due to scam awareness.

And yet, scams still proliferate — and they have been evolving along with technology. Smishing (SMS phishing) has been in the public consciousness for a while now, but have you heard of quishing? It essentially does the same thing, except that it’s done via QR codes.

Rappler researcher Lourence Angelo Marcellana listed 12 types of scams to watch out for, as we approach the holiday season. He also explained how to protect yourself against scams, especially since much of our transactions now happen online, thanks to the growth of e-commerce and digital payments.

In the GSMA report, it said that the Philippines also has the highest rate — among Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam — of reporting scams to digital platforms (49%), compared to only 16% reporting to the police. The regional average of reporting scams to the authorities is at 36%.

This reminded me of a Decoded study we did last year on online scams. We found that government agencies were among the most active sharers of warnings online, but because each agency’s approach lacked coordination with the others, the overall effect on consumers online was dissatisfaction from all the fragmented messaging.

Users online also complained about the government hotlines set up for reporting scams, saying that they found them difficult to use and lacking a clear process to submit evidence and receive updates on their cases.
That was last year. This year, the problem has now moved from how well the public is warned to knowing what kind of personal details may already be exposed, and who might be using them.

Last Friday, November 13, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) confirmed that personal data from around 20 state agencies were exposed in recent data breaches. Rappler researcher Alex Culla looked into these agencies and listed the personal information potentially exposed, from the Bureau of Internal Revenue, Securities and Exchange Commission, to the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation.

Among the personal details that may have been compromised are names, addresses, email addresses, mobile numbers, birth dates, genders, and even taxpayer identification numbers (TIN). Of course, these vary depending on the agency, and not everyone who deals with these agencies is necessarily affected. But it’s still worth staying alert, because while scams do happen all year, the CICC said it might become more prevalent as the holidays approach.
So if these recent leaks and scam warnings made you rethink your digital habits, there’s a place to start. At Rappler, Christmas isn’t the only thing we’re counting down to.

This year’s Social Good Summit is taking place this Saturday, November 21, and it will include a masterclass on data privacy and personal safety in the age of AI. There will also be discussions on technology, journalism, and human rights, as well as masterclasses on vibe coding, editorial cartooning, and crisis management.

articles.title: Fears grow over US sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.summary:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of…

blocks.text: Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

blocks.caption: A man cries during a protest in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, condemning violence against Rohingya people in Rakhine state, Myanmar. Photograph: Fazry Ismail/EPA

blocks.text: The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecuties individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu at a joint news conference in the White House last year. Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians”.
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
after newsletter promotion
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

blocks.caption: Palestinians search for bodies and survivors among the rubble in a destroyed area after Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, in October 2023. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA

blocks.text: In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically.”
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of the Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater US willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

articles.summary: This comes less than two weeks after US authorities arrested Markle in Florida on a federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs allegedly showing him with underage…

blocks.text: CRAME. The Philippine National Police headquarters at Camp Crame, Quezon City.
Jire Carreon/Rappler

This comes less than two weeks after US authorities arrested Markle in Florida on a federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs allegedly showing him with underage girls

MANILA, Philippines – Philippine police said on Wednesday, November 18, that criminal complaints had been filed against Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle, over alleged online child sexual abuse offenses.
The filing of the complaints will enable prosecutors to examine evidence and decide whether charges should be filed in court.

It came less than two weeks after US authorities arrested Markle in Florida on a federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs allegedly showing him with underage girls.
Thomas Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as “sick lies.”

Philippine police said complaints were filed before the prosecutor’s office in Cebu province on Monday, November 16, following an investigation last month into the alleged distribution and possession of child sexual abuse materials.
Markle had lived in Cebu for a period before returning to the United States.
Police said the complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children.

Forensic examination of the remaining devices surrendered in the Philippines by Markle’s son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr., was ongoing and could yield further evidence to support the case or lead to additional charges, if warranted, police said.
Meghan, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage ​to King Charles’ younger son, Harry, in 2018.
She has said she was “deeply distressed” over the matter. – Rappler.com
